text:
Lawyers for the Ecuadorian woman detained by federal agents at Denver International Airport this week have filed a habeas corpus petition challenging her arrest and confinement at the immigration detention facility in Aurora.

The Lichter Immigration law firm in Denver filed the federal petition Thursday on behalf of 27-year-old Chantal Alejandra Morales Rojas. Habeas petitions challenge someone’s incarceration, although not necessarily the underlying legal case that led to that confinement.

Under the Trump administration’s surge in immigration arrests and deportations, habeas petitions have become the predominant avenue for immigrants seeking release from detention.

A representative from U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday. The agency previously said Morales Rojas entered the U.S. on Oct. 20, 2024, and overstayed her visa, which allowed her to remain in the country until Jan. 4, 2025.

Video of Morales Rojas’ arrest at a Southwest Airlines gate at DIA on Monday has been widely shared on social media.

According to her attorneys, Morales Rojas entered the United States lawfully in January 2023 as a J-1 exchange visitor — a legal status allowing her to work as an au pair. She re-entered on a visa in 2024, according to her attorneys.

Before the end of the exchange program, Morales Rojas’ attorneys said she filed an application with U.S. immigration authorities allowing her to remain in the country while her case was under review. The application does not provide formal immigration status while she waits, the law firm said.

“During the last three and a half years, Morales Rojas lived openly in the United States with the government’s knowledge of her pending case, passed repeated background checks and received work authorization from (the Department of Homeland Security) while waiting for her application to be reviewed,” her attorneys said in a news release. “Morales Rojas has no criminal history or other concerns, and the process she’s pursuing is completely lawful.”

On Monday, ICE agents arrested Morales Rojas at DIA while she was boarding a flight back to Oakland, Calif., where she lives, after spending the weekend providing childcare for her former au pair family while they were at an ultimate Frisbee competition in Aurora.

Her law firm argues that the federal government knew who Morales Rojas was and where she lived and that she had a pending application with immigration authorities allowing her to be in the U.S. while under review. The application authorized the 27-year-old to work, and Morales Rojas has also been studying computer science, her lawyers said.

“You might not know it from watching the headlines for the last 18 months, but ICE generally can’t just arrest someone because they think they’re violating the immigration laws,” said lead attorney Laura L. Lichter. “They can put a case in front of an immigration judge if they think someone is here illegally, but unless there’s a special circumstance, they can’t legally detain someone without a proper arrest warrant and taking the time to review each case to see if a person is actually a flight risk or a danger.”

The petition asks the federal court to order Morales Rojas’ immediate release or require the government to provide the individualized custody determination required by law.

“This case is bigger than immigration policy,” Lichter said. “It’s about whether the government can take away a person’s liberty first and ask questions later. Habeas corpus exists to make sure that doesn’t happen.”

text:
“The Court finds that the Policy imposes a tax on H-1B petitions without the requisite delegation by Congress,” Judge Sorokin wrote.

What is the H-1B visa programme?

H-1B visas are meant for highly skilled workers in occupations where US employers struggle to find qualified American employees. The programme offers 65,000 visas annually, along with an additional 20,000 visas for applicants holding advanced US degrees. Successful applicants are typically granted visas valid for three to six years by the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

Before Trump’s proposed increase, employers sponsoring H-1B workers generally paid between $2,000 and $5,000 in government filing fees, depending on several factors.

Defending the fee hike, Trump had argued that the H-1B programme “has been deliberately exploited to replace, rather than supplement, American workers with lower-paid, lower-skilled labour.”

Who would have been affected?

The $100,000 fee would not have applied to foreign nationals already in the United States on student visas, who typically account for a large share of new H-1B recipients, according to Reuters.

The policy, announced in September 2025, significantly reduced demand for new H-1B petitions, Bloomberg reported. Court filings showed that by mid-February, the USCIS had received very few payments under the new fee structure.

States welcome the ruling

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell welcomed the appeals court’s decision, calling it a victory for employers that rely on highly skilled foreign workers.

“Today’s victory protects the integrity of the H-1B visa program as a tool to address severe labor shortages in vital industries like education, healthcare, and medical research,” Campbell said.

She added that the ruling would help Massachusetts fill critical vacancies and continue hiring world-class faculty members and researchers at colleges and universities across the state.

text:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker was dealt a major legal blow Friday after a federal judge gutted key state laws providing in-state tuition, financial aid and scholarships to illegal immigrants, marking another win for the Trump administration's nationwide immigration agenda.

U.S. District Judge Stephen McGlynn, a Trump appointee serving in the Southern District of Illinois, sided with the Justice Department, ruling that Illinois' in-state tuition policies, the RISE Act and the Illinois DREAM Act are "unconstitutional and invalid" as applied to illegal immigrants.

The ruling permanently prevents Illinois from enforcing the laws, although McGlynn delayed the order from taking effect for 14 days to allow the state to ask an appeals court to intervene.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUES COLORADO OVER IN-STATE TUITION AND FINANCIAL AID FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

U.S. Attorney Steven Weinhoeft celebrated the ruling.

"Illinois sought to incentivize illegal immigration on the taxpayer's dime by treating illegal aliens better than U.S. citizens living in other states, in clear violation of federal law," Weinhoeft said in a statement. "This ruling enforces the statute Congress wrote and stops the State from putting illegal aliens ahead of American citizens."

The decision is the latest victory for the Trump administration's effort to dismantle state laws extending higher education benefits to illegal immigrants and comes one day after the Justice Department filed a similar lawsuit against Colorado.

NEBRASKA ENDS IN-STATE TUITION BENEFITS FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS UNDER DOJ DEAL

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit against Illinois and a handful of colleges in September 2025, arguing that Illinois violated federal law by offering in-state tuition and financial aid to illegal immigrants without making those same benefits available to all U.S. citizens regardless of where they live.

McGlynn granted the federal government's motion for summary judgment and denied Illinois' motion to dismiss.

The ruling invalidates Illinois' in-state tuition rules, the RISE Act, which provides access to state financial aid for certain students ineligible for federal aid, and the Illinois DREAM Act, which established scholarship opportunities for eligible students.

DOJ ESCALATES BLUE-STATE ICE STANDOFF AFTER STATES REFUSE KEY FEDERAL REQUEST

Rep. Mary Miller, R-Ill. praised the decision on X.

"This is a win for Illinois taxpayers and American students who were shut out while Pritzker prioritized foreigners in our country illegally," Miller wrote.

The Justice Department has won or reached settlements in similar cases involving Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma and Nebraska, with Nebraska agreeing to end in-state tuition benefits for illegal immigrants as part of a settlement. Lawsuits remain pending against Minnesota, Virginia, California, New Jersey, Kansas, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maryland and now Colorado.

In its lawsuit filed Thursday against Colorado, the Justice Department argued the state's ASSET Act and related policies unlawfully provide lower tuition rates and state financial aid to illegal immigrants while denying those same benefits to out-of-state U.S. citizens.

"For three decades, Congress has made clear that Colorado cannot give education benefits to illegal aliens that it does not give to all American citizens," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said. "By granting illegal aliens in-state tuition, Colorado is not only violating federal law but subsidizing education for illegal aliens at taxpayers' expense."

"Our litigation efforts will not cease until we have fulfilled President Trump's promise that illegal aliens will not obtain preferential treatment over our nation's own citizens," he added.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis' office defended the state's policies.

You'll be able to continue working" Mills told Information Morning.
Her client Luca Ferrante's permanent residency journey has been ongoing for almost seven years.

text:
Some Nova Scotia business owners say Canada's move to rein in immigration and reduce pathways to permanent residency is creating challenges for their companies and they're calling for a policy overhaul.

Dave Culligan, the owner of Threesixfive Media, told CBC Radio's Information Morning Nova Scotia that one of his best employees, video content specialist Zen Sun, was forced to leave Canada and return to China.

Culligan said Sun had lived in Canada for seven years and worked for him for three.

"It's hard these days to run a small company, so it was devastating," Culligan said.

Culligan said Sun had studied at NSCAD and stood out in a competitive application process.

"He just brought a great attitude, and pre-existing and always-developing skill sets to our team. And this is someone that never complained, always gave their best, always took care of their teammates and someone that frankly, I grew to love."

Before he left, Sun and Culligan worked on a video to draw attention to the immigration issue. The video features local business owners and workers from outside Canada who are trying to stay.

'A lot of confusion in the system'

In the video, Sun said he believed that if he and other immigrants "contributed, stayed patient and followed the rules, there would be a future for us here."

Culligan said he doesn't understand the federal government's reasoning for denying Sun and others like him a pathway to permanent citizenship.

"It feels like there's a lack of communication, a lack of clarity and just a lot of confusion in the system," he said.

"... There's hundreds of stories of folks who are being told one thing and then hearing another and policies change, so these people are being left in limbo."

Mike Mills, president and CEO at Cabco Communications Group, also participated in the video.

He said he went through a similar situation with two employees who had been in Canada for about five years, both waiting on their permanent residency, but their work permits were expiring.

"The thought was always [if] you're on a work permit waiting on your [permanent residency] application status, it's going to get renewed. You'll be able to continue working" Mills told Information Morning.

But that didn't happen. In April, he said both employees were "effectively told they have 90 days to leave the country."

'It's a business issue, it's a humanity issue'

Mills posted about the experience on LinkedIn and Culligan reached out about making the video.

"It's a business issue, it's a humanity issue. I feel really badly about how these immigrants are being treated. It seems like the ground has shifted. Nobody knows exactly what the rules are," Mills said.

"It's almost like they signed up for a race. They knew it was going to be challenging, but there was a finish line and now there's no finish line and there's a chance that they get pulled off the course mid-race and sent home."

Mills said this is hurting businesses too.

"We invest in these employees. There's training involved. It takes a while for employees to ramp up and become kind of a core part of your business and when they lose their work permits, you're basically starting over," Mills said.

While Ottawa is expanding its Express Entry immigration program for some skilled workers, Mills said the focus needs to be on people who are currently working.

"These are people who've been in the country for a number of years. They've been following the process. They should receive some clarity about where they stand," he said.

CBC News requested an interview with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, but did not receive a response in time for publication.

Indefinite waiting periods

Sarah McInnes, an immigration lawyer for McInnes Cooper, told Information Morning that Mills's comments echo what she hears from clients and employers in recent years.

McInnes said some of her clients are waiting "indefinitely" to hear about their permanent residency.

Her client Luca Ferrante's permanent residency journey has been ongoing for almost seven years.

Ferrante owns Sapori Italian Street Food, a restaurant on the Halifax waterfront where he employs four people permanently and 15 people part-time for the summer. He is on his fourth work permit since arriving in Canada and it's set to expire in October.

"We're running a business so we love what we do, but ... stress about the work permit insecurity sometimes makes things a little bit more complicated," Ferrante, who is originally from Italy, told Information Morning.

At one point, his application for a work permit was rejected so he had to leave Canada to speed up the timeline so he could go back to work faster.

Ferrante said it wasn't clear why his work permit was rejected. McInnes said rejections can be brief and generic.

Small errors can derail application

"The smallest administrative error on an application can lead to a refusal. And that's what happened," McInnes said.

When a work permit is refused, McInnes said you have to stop working immediately. She said that can be challenging for Canadian businesses who rely on these employees.

McInnes says the federal government should flag errors to applicants so they can be fixed and resubmitted, and that people should be allowed to continue working while the change is made.

She said it's unlikely Ferrante will get his permanent residency status by October, so they'll be going for a work permit again.

While work permits are processed, she said Luca will be in "maintained status" for a four-to-five-month period, which means he'll be able to work, but won't be able to leave the country.

"They cannot leave or they risk their status and this goes on for months at a time. So if there's any family emergency at home or any reason that they have to leave, they cannot," McInnes said.

'I have my life here'

Despite the struggle, Ferrante said he would like to stay in Canada.

"I would love to stay here. Since we came, we fell in love with the culture, we love the city of Halifax, the people are great. So we really hope we'll find a way to stay," he said.

He said if he can't stay, he'll be forced to sell the business and go back to Italy.

"That would be sad because my co-workers are my friends and I have a good number of regular customers who come all the time ... I have my life here.”

text:
A chaotic scene unfolded in San Diego’s City Heights neighborhood Thursday as activists and protesters descended on an area where federal agents had been spotted.

The incident unfolded in the intersection of Fairmount and Maple in the early afternoon. People who carry out community patrols across San Diego to warn residents of the possible presence of ICE agents said they received tips late that morning that agents were there, and headed to the area.

“We saw at least six different ICE vehicles roaming, swarming the area, and that is an act of hostility and intimidation,” said Benjamin Prado, of Union Del Barrio, an organization that does those patrols. “We began to document and demand that they leave our communities.”

ICE directed questions to Customs and Border Protection, who said they were looking into the incident but did not share specifics on what the agents were doing.

One resident, who asked not to be identified, said it all began when the agents’ truck wouldn’t start and they were waiting for a tow.

Videos show dozens of people screaming, using bullhorns and sirens. That resident called it “a melee” and said the people encroaching on his lawn became confrontational, so he called San Diego police.

SDPD said they received the call around 1:54 p.m. over the crowd forming around a federal vehicle, noting that a window had been broken on the truck. Police said it was unknown who broke the window or how, but two witnesses said it was someone in the crowd with a slingshot.

“SDPD officers responded to the scene and worked to maintain the peace. The federal agents left shortly after SDPD officers arrived,” San Diego police said in a statement. “SDPD was on scene for approximately 20 minutes until the vehicle had been towed.”

Some said they were upset to see San Diego police at the scene at all, with videos showing people in the crowd chanting that SDPD was assisting ICE. SDPD said they were not participating in federal immigration enforcement, in accordance with California law that bars the use of state and local law enforcement resources in that capacity.

A few who gathered in the street can be heard on video asking San Diego police officers for their badge numbers. Some protesters said they were frustrated at what appeared to be the officers’ refusal.

The SDPD policy manual says, “Officers shall furnish their names and Department member identification numbers to any person requesting this information when they are on duty or while representing the Department in an official capacity, except when the withholding of such information is necessary for the performance of police duties or is authorized by the proper authority.”

Of one such encounter captured on video, SDPD said in a statement the officer “was focused on safely managing the chaotic scene. It is clear from the video that there are multiple people yelling, making it difficult for anyone to reasonably engage and respond. His name is clearly displayed on the front of his uniform.”

"If they're there to protect and serve, then they need to tell the agents to leave our communities," Prado said, adding that he believed no one was detained as the incident unfolded.

“My block isn’t like this. This is a nice, quiet little neighborhood,” said one neighbor, who also asked not to be identified. She said she’s lived in the area for decades and watched the incident unfold before heading inside, afraid it would escalate. “I don’t know which ones were agitators and which ones weren’t.”

“It’s kind of scary, but our world right now is scary, because this is supposed to be the land of the free,” she continued. “Everybody’s got rights.”

text:
“Honestly, in that moment, I did not understand what was going on, what was happening to me,” Sister Leticia Ugboaja said at a news conference at Our Lady of Sorrows Church in McAllen, where she spoke out for the first time since U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested her on June 28.

Ugboaja’s attorney says she has for years been granted protection from removal to her native Nigeria because she was likely to face torture there.

Ugboaja, 56, was released several hours after being detained while on her way to church near the U.S.-Mexico border. Parish officials’ posting about her on social media brought attention to her case, and Congress members ultimately intervened on her behalf. President Donald Trump made mass deportations a central promise of his second administration, with his immigration crackdown leading to unusually aggressive tactics that have faced scrutiny.

Ugboaja, who has a check-in appointment with ICE on Tuesday, said she wanted to speak out to help others, and pleaded for people to have the chance to be heard before being taken into custody.

“There are many others in this same situation, people who have been given some form of protection under our laws, who have followed every rule asked of them, and who still live with uncertainty,” Ugboaja said.

While she’s grateful to those who helped her, she said, that “does not mean I can stay quiet about what happened to me, or about what is still happening to others.”

Her attorney, Carlos M. Garcia, sat next to Ugboaja at the news conference and provided details about her immigration case. He said that in 2019 an immigration judge denied her application for asylum but granted her protection from removal to Nigeria because she likely would be tortured there. Garcia said Ugboaja, who is a nurse, has complied with everything required of her and had permission to work in the U.S.

When ICE detained Ugboaja in June, she wasn’t given much explanation as to why she was taken into custody, her attorney said. But the U.S. planned to remove her to a third country, he added.

The Trump administration’s third-country removal policy has been criticized by lawyers and human rights groups and has faced legal challenges. The Department of Homeland Security has said the agreements allow people seeking asylum in the U.S. to pursue protection in the other country, and that the agreements are used to try to address large backlogs in immigration courts.

DHS and ICE did not respond to a request to comment on Ugboaja’s case on Thursday and did not respond to requests for comment after her detention in June.

Ugboaja is part of the Daughters of Mary Mother of Mercy and volunteered as an Extraordinary Minister of Holy Communion at Our Lady of Sorrows Church, a spokesperson for the Diocese of Brownsville has said. Ugboaja is also a registered nurse at South Texas Health System and worked previously for 10 years as a certified nursing assistant in Edinburg, the spokesperson said.

Ugboaja said that on the day she was taken into custody, she begged the officers to let her attend Mass and receive Holy Communion, but was told she could not.

“For me, a nun, not to go to Mass on Sunday, not to receive Communion, it was very, very heartbreaking for me,” she said.

___

Stengle reported from Dallas.

text:
As state leaders took the first step to force local police to comply with a new law banning them from working with federal immigration officials, Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman blasted the policy with the family of an 18-year-old from Yorktown who was killed in Chicago by an undocumented man earlier this year.

Blakeman on Friday stood with the parents of Sheridan Gorman, a Loyola University Chicago freshman who died in March. “Stop normalizing what happened to Sheridan Gorman – it’s not normal,” Blakeman said at the campaign event in Yorktown, in Westchester County. “When I become governor, the first executive order I will sign on day one is: New York state is no longer a sanctuary state.”

Blakeman, who is also the Nassau County executive, and Gorman’s family were additionally joined by Rep. Mike Lawler, who’s facing one of the nation’s toughest reelection bids in the battleground 17th Congressional District. Both were moved to tears by Gorman’s parents.

“Elections decide whether laws are enforced, whether police are empowered and whether families like ours are protected, or whether they’re left to bury the consequences,” Jessica Gorman said.

At almost the same time, state Attorney General Letitia James’ office sent letters to 12 local law enforcement agencies that have formal partnerships with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement known as a 287(g) agreement. Agencies included the Nassau County Police Department and the Madison County Sheriff's Department, led by Blakemans’ running mate Todd Hood. The agreements can include sharing information, deputizing local police officers to enforce civil immigration law or using local jails for immigration enforcement. A new law expanding protections for immigrants will require all 12 agencies to end their partnerships with ICE by Aug. 25.

All 12 agencies must respond to the letter about the status of their agreement by Aug. 14.

The new law has stirred controversy and drawn the attention of the federal government. The U.S. Department of Justice sued Hochul and James over the policy last month. State officials filed a counter federal suit as a defensive mechanism, asking the court to uphold the legislative package as a defensive measure on the same day.

Blakeman said he has spoken with other county officials who have similar agreements, and they’re exploring their separate legal options to react to the legislation. He added he has not taken action to change his county’s 287(g) agreement to date. “The lawyers for our police department and sheriff’s department are reviewing the law and the attorney general’s letter, and we will have a written response by Aug. 14,” Blakeman told City & State in a statement after the Yorktown event.

Immigration policies at both the state and federal level remain at the forefront of the gubernatorial race and high-stakes midterm elections – especially as Republicans vie to maintain control of the U.S. House of Representatives.

“If you don’t want ICE to be a necessity, if you don’t want ICE to be surging in your communities, it’s very simple: Seal the border and cooperate when it comes to criminal aliens,” Lawler said. “Then you really won’t have any of these issues.”

Hochul’s office argued that the new immigration law, called the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, bars local police from entering into 287(g) agreements, but does not prohibit the state Department of Corrections and Community Supervision, nor local jails, from coordinating with ICE in criminal matters. If New York’s new policy had been in effect in Illinois, it would not have affected the jail's ability to turn over a detainee to ICE in the case of Sheridan Gorman, according to Hochul’s office.

"The murder of Sheridan Gorman is a tragedy, and if found guilty the man responsible should serve the maximum sentence and then be deported,” a spokesperson with Hochul’s office said in a statement. “But the way we keep New Yorkers safe is by focusing our local law enforcement on actual criminals, not assisting in ICE operations that harass innocent people and split apart families.”

text:
Last fall, life for the Perez children was turned upside down. Their father, Romeo Sr., was picked up on his way to work and sent to immigration detention. A few months later, their mother, Olga, was detained, too. Her daughter was driving when they were pulled over. Romeo Sr. and Olga were both undocumented and had lived in the United States for decades; their children are US citizens.

“I just remember after he had started banging on the window, like, telling me that I have to put the windows down so my mom and my uncle can give their IDs,” says 21-year old Eliza Perez. She told the officer, “You took my dad, and now you’re taking my mom.”

With their parents gone, Eliza, Jessica, Romeo Jr., and Cynthia had to fend for themselves in Lake Worth, Florida. Eliza, a college student, took charge of the household and the family’s landscaping business.

The Perezes are not alone. An estimated 205,000 kids have had a parent detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the last year and a half. It’s happening all over the country and, in some cases, to the same families who were separated at the border during the first Trump administration.

This week on Reveal, filmmakers Max Maldonado and José Jesús Zaragoza and Mother Jones reporters Samantha Michaels and Isabela Dias look into the lives of two families fighting to stay together as the Trump administration’s deportation agenda rips them apart.

text:
(NewsNation) — A Kenyan national who played briefly with the National Football League’s Indianapolis Colts has been deported by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Chicago after he was previously ordered to leave the United States.

Daniel Ogama Adongo, 37, overstayed his visa in 2016 after his NFL career ended in 2015. A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered him removed March 23, and ICE deported him June 20, the agency announced Friday.

Adongo was arrested multiple times in Indiana over the past nine years for crimes including felony intimidation, battery and disorderly conduct. He was convicted of criminal mischief with damage in 2020 and sentenced to 364 days in jail, federal prosecutors said.

Adongo, a former rugby player who turned to football, was released by the Colts in 2015 after he played a total of five games, mostly on special teams. His release came after police were called to a home in suburban Indianapolis to check on a woman who lived at the residence with Adongo, ESPN reported.

According to a police report, the woman notified a friend via text message that she needed help. The friend got in touch with the police, who then arrived at the residence. There, the woman said she did not want medical assistance, and she could not explain why she sent the text, the report indicated.

The most recent criminal charges fall under the Laken Riley Act, which requires the detention, without bond, of migrants in the U.S. illegally for certain crimes.

The bill was introduced following the murder of Laken Riley by a migrant who had previously been cited for shoplifting on the University of Georgia campus in Athens, Georgia. President Trump signed the bill into law shortly after taking office in 2025.

Trump administration officials have reported that more than 356,000 people have been deported in fiscal year 2026 while ICE arrests have increased significantly since May.

“This dangerous individual was clearly a threat to the community, which is now safer since he’s been removed,” ICE Chicago Assistant Field Office Director Douglas Thompson said in a statement released by the Department of Homeland Security. “Those who violate immigration law are held equally accountable, including former professional athletes.”

text:
Someone driving on Highway 211 east of Woodburn in Clackamas County last Friday afternoon spotted a vehicle with flashing red and blue lights behind them.

Thinking police were conducting a traffic stop, the driver pulled over and stopped.

Two men, one of whom was armed with a rifle, got out of the vehicle and told the driver they were with ICE and that the driver was being detained.

The two men forced the driver out of the car and placed them in the back of their vehicle, where a third man guarded the driver and assaulted them.

The men wore tactical vests with “POLICE” written on them.

After about 15 or 20 minutes, the men let the driver go.

But according to Oregon State Police, the men were not real law enforcement officers.

But the ruse apparently continued even after the fake traffic stop.

The victim later went to a hospital to be treated for injuries received during the incident. While there, OSP said the victim began receiving text messages claiming to represent a law firm offering to help in the matter.

OSP said the messages came from the phone number 971-502-5548.

ALSO READ: Portland leaders debate banning police masks, identifying federal agents

OSP said it confirmed with federal law enforcement agencies that no federal agents were involved in the incident.

The people pretending to be law enforcement officers were reported to be wearing boots, baseball caps, face coverings and green long-sleeve shirts, OSP said.

The men were also carrying badges marked “Police.”

They were driving a newer model and smaller blue or gray SUV. It had no visible license plates.

OSP said it and the FBI are investigating the reported incident.

State police said they want to hear from anyone who saw suspicious activity in the area of Highway 211 near South Barlow Road on July 17 or anyone who may have encountered people impersonating law enforcement.

They also want to hear from anyone who has received similar messages from the phone number 971-502-5548.

Those with information are asked to call OSP dispatch at 800-442-0776 or *OSP (*677) from a mobile phone and reference case number SP26-237961.

ALSO READ: Gov. Ferguson signs bills banning police impersonators, law enforcement wearing masks

In its news release on Friday, OSP offered the following tips to protect yourself when you’re unsure you are being pulled over by a real law enforcement officer.

title: As Haitian protections near Monday expiration date, workers, employers battle uncertainty ...
description:

“Like all U.S. employers, Areas is required to comply with federal law and employment-eligibility requirements,” the spokesperson said.
“A large number of them have Temporary Protected Status employees from various countries over many years of doing business in South Florida.
“A good portion,” she said, support the health care system in South Florida as nurses and care workers.

text:
As a pep rally for Haitian immigrant airport workers gained steam earlier this month, a labor union official complained that many of her local’s 170 members who work there weren’t receiving the employer support they need to retain their Temporary Protected Status, which is targeted for elimination by the U.S. Government.

Despite a succession of last-minute extensions by federal immigration authorities, time appears to be finally running out for thousands of Haitian immigrants in South Florida. Come Monday, employers across the region’s health care, hospitality, and construction sectors face a potential hard deadline to terminate staff who rely on Temporary Protected Status. With the Trump administration pushing to eliminate the program, local trade groups are begging Washington for more time so these workers can figure out another legal way to stay.

The tension is already boiling over at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. During the rally on July 10, Wendi Walsh, secretary-treasurer of UNITE Here Local 355, reeled off the names of several concession operators and accused them of remaining silent as the administration fought in the courts.

“There is one group who is not in this room today,” declared Walsh. “There is a clear silence among our employers who should be standing up for our workers. This is an airport full of Haitian workers … we are listening and we hear nothing about you standing up for your workers.”

Then she called out one of the biggest employers at the airport: Areas USA, which operates restaurants at airports, rail stations, and roadside rest areas.

“We heard nothing from Areas USA,” Walsh told her audience. “Instead they are terminating people today.”

Around the nation that Friday, there were reports of widespread firings of Haitians as employers operated under the assumption that July 10 was the final TPS termination date in a long line of such dates. But then, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services quietly announced on its website that another extension was in play, this time until July 24.

Areas USA, reached after the rally for comment, declined to discuss its airport employees’ status, citing privacy considerations.

But in a statement, a spokesperson said the company is focused on following federal law.

“Like all U.S. employers, Areas is required to comply with federal law and employment-eligibility requirements,” the spokesperson said. “When federal law no longer permits an individual to work, we cannot legally continue their employment, and any resulting action is based solely on the absence of legally required work authorization.

“Areas will continue to employ every individual who remains legally authorized to work, and we are consistently monitoring guidance from USCIS and the Department of Homeland Security, including any judicial or administrative developments that may affect the July 27 date,” she said, citing the latest date in which the government can act to end TPS for Haitians. “We are communicating directly with potentially affected employees and are committed to complying with the law while treating every team member with dignity, consistency, and respect.”

It is not known what the company and others that employ Haitian workers in South Florida plan to do this time. Industry trade groups including the Florida Health Care Association and Florida Restaurant and Lodging Association have asked the government to allot more time so members can make work force adjustments and/or help the affected Haitian workers find alternate ways to stay in the U.S.

Determined administration

The government itself appears to have kept its own counsel in the face of those requests. Its actions, however, make it clear that it remains steadfast in its determination to end TPS programs for not only Haitians, but also for those allowing other foreign national groups to remain in the U.S.

On Wednesday, a Republican-dominated U.S. Senate blocked an effort by Democrats to adopt a House action designed to extend TPS for Haitians another three years.

Even before the vote and with the Supreme Court decision in hand, the government reportedly started twice-a-week deportation flights to Haiti.

On Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security announced more than 100 people with criminal backgrounds had been returned to the Caribbean nation on July 16 aboard a deportation flight.

“Last week, ICE deported pedophiles, carjackers, drug traffickers and perpetrators of fraud to Haiti,” Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis said in a news release. “Criminal illegal aliens have NO place in American communities. Our message to illegal aliens is clear: LEAVE NOW. If you don’t, we will find you and deport you.”

In late June, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the Department of Homeland Security could finally terminate Temporary Protected Status for Haiti, an exercise that started last summer only to become immersed in court challenges from rights groups representing immigrants. The court held that the TPS statute bars judicial review of non-constitutional challenges to the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decisions to extend or terminate Temporary Protected Status.

The court also concluded that the people challenging the end of the Haiti TPS designation were not likely to succeed on their equal protection claims, which are still being pursued by lawyers. They have until July 31 to possibly amend their complaint to include discrimination claims on the Haitians’ behalf. But those claims, the Supreme Court itself declared, are unlikely to succeed.

But this past Wednesday, the Trump administration was denied a request by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to end the program Friday. The court promptly set this Monday, July 27, as the date when the Administration can cancel TPS for Haitians.

Bureaucratic “fire drill”

Companies and their legal advisors have found it next to impossible to keep pace.

“We’ve been running this fire drill for the past couple of weeks,” said Stefanie Camfield, associate general counsel for Hollywood-based Engage PEO, an employment law advisory firm for businesses. “July 1 then the 10th, the 24th and now the 27th. All of this confusion for employers is really frustrating. I literally weeks ago had to tell my clients, ‘you have to wait and see.’ They keep pushing the date back.”

“If somebody has a work authorization, you can’t terminate them,” she added. “You can end up with a national origin discrimination claim.”

“Employers are expected to keep an eye on this. I don’t know how a small business owner can keep up. I’m having trouble keeping up and I’ve been practicing law for 18 years,” Camfield said. “I feel for the people whose employees are directly impacted. Employers are stuck in this impossible situation. They want to help [workers] however they can but they can’t continue to employ them once the work authorizations are terminated.”

Fear and confusion across industries

For decades, Haitians have migrated to South Florida from their Caribbean nation to escape authoritarian rule, organized gang violence, assassinations, kidnappings, military interventions, disease, and natural disasters.

The TPS now in force was authorized in 2010 after an earthquake flattened cities and killed thousands. Conservative critics in the U.S. argue that Haiti TPS has gone beyond temporary and become permanent through repeated renewals. Advocates counter the danger and suffering endured by Haitians in their homeland that has been continuous and far from temporary.

Hopes that an estimated 350,000 Haitian immigrants would be allowed to remain in the United States past the summer were deflated by the Supreme Court ruling and in Congress, where the U.S. Senate on Wednesday refused to consider a House action that would have extended their stays for three years.

In the interim, South Florida industries served by thousands of Haitian immigrants — such as health care, hospitality, construction and transportation — are finding it difficult to manage.

“I have had many calls from various tourism and hospitality industry venues, businesses, and owners,” said Peter Ricci, director of the hospitality and tourism management program at the Florida Atlantic University College of Business. “A large number of them have Temporary Protected Status employees from various countries over many years of doing business in South Florida. All are concerned about the loss of these individuals and their potential need to replace the workers. Further, there are simply the ‘human concerns’ with many of them being long-term employees, often over a period of many years.

“The main concern at this point is the ongoing change of time for their workers,” Ricci said in an email to the South Florida Sun Sentinel. “If they had a firm date, many are willing to assist their current TPS-protected workers with return-to-country flight assistance or other manners. However, with the extensions [being] somewhat of a ‘moving target’ in terms of dates, they are equally frustrated.”

He noted that for an industry that staffs hotels and restaurants based on anticipated visitor volume, not knowing whether workers will be available to fill a one- or two-week work schedule “is confounding to operators.”

Candice Mondesir, executive director of the Haitian-American Chamber of Commerce of Florida, said in an interview that the impact of ousting thousands of Haitians will be felt far beyond the labor market.

Haitian immigrants, she said, contribute $2.6 billion to the statewide economy.

“A good portion,” she said, support the health care system in South Florida as nurses and care workers. “A lot of hospitals hire Haitian TPS workers — they run very heavily into nursing.”

Throughout Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties, many own businesses and hold home mortgages and car loans.

“They’re entrepreneurs,” Mondesir said. “They pay taxes like everybody else. What happens when you say, ‘this person is not legally here’? What happens to the Social Security number and the money they paid into Social Security? A lot of times there are so many different things that I don’t think people are looking at the full blown picture. It’s a whole ecosystem that is going to be disrupted.”

In the streets of cities such as North Miami and North Miami Beach, “you see them affected by it. A lot of the businesses are struggling because people are afraid to come out.”

“Parents are scared to send kids to school in August,” Mondesir added. “There’s a lot coming down the pipeline and it’s terrifying.”

Contingency planning abounds, she said, with many people examining the possibility of moving to Canada because that nation “has an easy pathway to citizenship and residency.”

Narrow options ahead

State Rep. Marie Woodson, a Democrat whose district includes Hollywood and Pembroke Pines, aired what many supporters of the Haitian community have been advocating: action by Congress that will provide a long-term extension of TPS and a pathway to citizenship.

““Give them a path to citizenship, that’s what they need, especially people with no criminal records,” said Woodson. She migrated to South Florida from Haiti in 1981, when the country was ruled by dictator Jean-Claude “Baby Doc” Duvalier, who became “President for Life” after the death of his father, François Duvalier.

“The situation to me, it’s more than concerning,” Woodson said. “It’s heart-wrenching to me. You have human beings — law-abiding people who came here legally and they have made a life, which means a lot of them are working.”

On Friday, some lawmakers reportedly met with immigration law experts and community leaders to discuss legal options, as well as ways to keep people safe if Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents start a deportation roundup.

Renata Castro, a longtime immigration lawyer based in Coral Springs, forecast a long road of arrests and litigation.

“Once the TPS expires, I believe that the government is going to detain people very rapidly just to spread fear in the community,” she said. “And after that, as litigation goes forward you will see people released as injunctions will be granted. I wouldn’t be surprised if we get to a place where litigation of this case will end only when we have a new president, which I wouldn’t complain about.”

Countdown to the End of Haiti TPS

text:
Washington health inspectors are once again temporarily blocked from entering the Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in Tacoma in an ongoing legal battle between the state and the private prison company that operates the facility, GEO Group.

Judges William Fletcher, Ronald Gould and Jacqueline Nguyen with the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted an administrative stay Tuesday, effectively pausing a U.S. District Court order that would have allowed Department of Health inspectors inside the facility.

The stay, which came two days before inspectors could have gone in, will last until judges hear more from both sides and make a decision.

The continued pause was expected. On July 9, when U.S. District Judge Benjamin Settle sided with the state and granted preliminary injunctions to allow inspections of the detention center, he ordered that the injunctions wouldn’t take effect for two weeks to allow time for an appeal.

This week, GEO Group asked the 9th Circuit to stay the lower court’s decision. It argued ICE is prohibiting health inspectors — not GEO Group — and that federal rules on immigration enforcement trump state law. ICE, which is at the center of the dispute, is not a party in this case.

The Northwest ICE Processing Center, about a mile from downtown Tacoma, is one of the largest facilities of its kind nationwide, with more than 1,500 beds.

GEO Group is one of the most profitable private prison companies in the world. The Florida-based company, founded by George Zoley, is worth over $4 billion. Zoley immigrated to the U.S. from Greece when he was 3 years old.

The administrative stay comes a day after a Colorado man, employed by GEO Group, was charged with assault for allegedly shooting an anti-ICE protester outside an ICE detention facility run by GEO Group near Denver.

Since Washington passed a law in 2023 setting health and safety standards for private detention centers in the state and allowing unannounced inspections from the Department of Health, GEO Group has prevented health officials from inspecting the center.

After receiving over 3,500 complaints from detained people about conditions at the facility, Attorney General Nick Brown’s office asked the court in April to issue an order permitting state health officials to enter and inspect the building.

At the detention center, people have reported inadequate medical care, black mold in showers, unsafe drinking water, laundry returned wet and dirtier than before and food containing “burned plastic, metal string, splinters, hair, and worms.”

GEO Group and ICE did not immediately respond to requests for comments.

text:
Transcript

TAMARA KEITH, HOST:

Immigration has been a motivating issue for Republicans for every election, going back years. But aggressive immigration tactics have shifted public opinion. So how is immigration playing in this year's midterm campaigns? We've got some early answers.

(SOUNDBITE OF THE BIGTOP ORCHESTRA'S "TEETER BOARD: FOLIES BERGERE (MARCH AND TWO-STEP)")

KEITH: It's the NPR POLITICS PODCAST. I'm Tamara Keith. I cover politics.

XIMENA BUSTILLO, BYLINE: I'm Ximena Bustillo, and I cover immigration policy.

MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: And I'm Mara Liasson, senior national political correspondent.

KEITH: Ximena, there have been two fatal shootings this month involving ICE officers, first in Texas, then last week in Maine. How have those incidents altered the conversation over immigration enforcement?

BUSTILLO: Right. It had been a few months since there had been some sort of direct interaction and clash of this kind pretty much since Minneapolis, which was in January of this year when two U.S. citizens were killed. Now, in this instance, both were - you know, both were men. Both were fathers. Both were people who were in vehicles at the time that they were shot both by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, neither was the target of the arrests. And so this has renewed conversations about the tactics, the training, the direction and directive that these ICE officers are being given to result in deaths of individuals who are not even the target of the arrests.

KEITH: And you mentioned it, but both of these incidents involve traffic stops, and that has gotten a lot of focus. And for a moment there, it seemed like there might have even been talk of a policy shift.

BUSTILLO: Yeah. There was a brief about 24 hours, maybe, if that, where there seemed to be directive coming from Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin to put a stop to all traffic stops. Now, it is important to note that traffic stops are extremely common when it comes to immigration arrests. Like, that is one of the primary ways, actually, that these arrests take place. And there had been a lot of controversy about the types of warrants that ICE was using to enter homes. And so, in order to not go to people's homes or do a lot of door knocking where people might not answer, they were doing a lot more traffic stops. But to your point, right after it seemed like that directive was handed to pause, put a freeze on traffic stops, very quickly, the president came out and said that he did not like that and actually wanted them to restart that policy.

KEITH: Yeah, and he in this Truth Social post, wrote, we cannot give up one of ICE's most important and effective crime fighting tools - traffic stops. So that was a very quick policy reversal.

BUSTILLO: Yes. And, you know, this comes at a time in which Mullin wanted to take ICE out of the headlines. Mullin has done, I think, a lot to, you know, make sure that the agency is still following through on this mass deportation promise. We are still seeing high, record numbers of people in immigration detention, which means they're still detaining people, and they're still processing people out for deportations. But you're just not seeing the big surges on cities like we saw in Boston and Chicago, LA, Minneapolis, like, nearly a year ago.

LIASSON: Yeah. And also, the other thing that's driving this is that we have reports that ICE has been given some very ambitious quotas for how many arrests they're expected to make. And that's also driving this, you know, one, 2,000 a day. And that's why even though Mullin wanted ICE out of the headlines, these incidents are still happening because ICE is just as aggressive as ever, and now they have the added pressure of the White House telling them how many arrests they need to accomplish.

KEITH: In quick order.

LIASSON: In quick order, yeah.

KEITH: And, Ximena, in the policy realm, another issue that has come up in connection with these shootings is that the officers were not wearing body cams - body worn cameras. Didn't the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE and Border Patrol commit to having officers wear body cameras earlier this year, wasn't there, like, a lot of money for that?

BUSTILLO: Yes and no. I mean, anyone can commit to trying to do anything, and that was essentially what former secretary Kristi Noem did after the two shootings in Minneapolis, was she said every officer and agent in Minneapolis would get one, keeping in mind that they very quickly did scale that back, just the number of people that were there, and that they would have an effort to do some sort of broader expansion nationwide. There has long been a lot of complaints from the agency that there just simply wasn't the money for the body cameras. So Congress did fix that in a sense.

So in April, one of the spending packages did include $20 million just for body-worn cameras. Now, DHS then says that they were shut down, so yeah, maybe they got the money, but they couldn't do the implementation. They couldn't get the contracts out. They couldn't do the training. Like, all these other things because they were shut down, they couldn't do. Then they get another $31 billion for technology, which included body cameras, so not just body cameras, but Congress did lay it out. This was one of the things you can spend these billions on. And the thing to keep in mind here, though, is they are not mandating. There's no law that says that ICE officers and Border Patrol agents have to be wearing them. And there's not really a whole lot of a policy that mandates that either because the agency just hasn't had enough to extensively require it.

LIASSON: To simplify the politics of this, the Democrats were pushing very hard for legislation that would require body cams, no face masks, judicial warrants to do certain kinds of entries into buildings. And that didn't pass. So there is money for all these things if ICE wanted to do them. Democrats say since no requirement that any of those things get done, that's why you see these incidents happening again and again where someone is killed, but there's no video record because there's no body cam. And that used to be the frontline of the immigration policy debate in Congress, whether you're going to not necessarily abolish ICE but reform it by requiring ICE agents to wear body cams, have warrants and not have face masks.

BUSTILLO: And to Mara's point, you know, the body camera requirement was pretty bipartisan. There are Republicans that, especially after these two shootings, have said they need to have body cameras. Like, there are plenty of studies that also show body cameras often, you know, justify the action of the law enforcement officer as well. So it really kind of benefits all the parties to have increased transparency.

Now, the latest that the White House and DHS has said is that about half of all field offices have them and they're in the process of, you know, getting them out to the rest of everyone. I believe White House boarder czar Tom Homan said that the trainers are being trained on how to train officers to use the cameras. And so this is going to take a while. I mean, there are a lot of competing timelines. ICE Director David Venturella said that by the end of July, these would all be handed out. There's another 60 day time frame that's kind of floating around. So, you know, it's going to take a while for everyone to fully get a functioning body camera, be using it in their day to day. Like, this is not going to happen in a matter of days.

KEITH: So let's bring this to the realm of politics. Maine, where this most recent shooting took place, has a hotly contested U.S. Senate race. Incumbent Susan Collins is running for reelection, and Democrats are hoping to flip her seat. Has this shooting come up in that race?

LIASSON: Yes, it certainly has. Susan Collins, who is the chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, she funds DHS and ICE. Democrats are saying she bears a special responsibility for this because she voted for that bill, $70 billion for ICE without requiring body cameras, warrants and no face masks. Susan Collins, for her part, is trying to focus on Democrats who call for abolishing ICE because that's not necessarily a popular position, but body cameras, warrants and no face masks are.

One of the things that has been really driving Democrats crazy in Maine is that Susan Collins called for an investigation of the shooting. She also said it was, quote, "extremely unfortunate," and Democrats say this is her usual response. She never really pushed back against Trump unless it doesn't matter, unless there're already the votes. And they are trying to connect her with all the parts of the Trump administration that are unpopular. She is a Republican. She's voted for most of them. But she's trying to focus on the parts of the Democratic immigration agenda that are not popular, like abolished ICE. And that's at least what the front-runner for the Democratic Senate Troy Jackson is calling for. He's an abolished ICE guy.

KEITH: And that convention to decide who will be the party's nominee is this weekend. Troy Jackson appears to have locked it up, and he is definitely in the progressive lane. And he joined protests against the ICE shooting immediately following it, along with some of the other Senate candidates.

LIASSON: I think the trick, really, in Maine is that as long as the shooting is front and center and that's what people are thinking about, it's bad for Collins. But if that quiets down and we're back to these kind of slightly more abstract policy discussions, should we reform ICE or abolish it, then I think Collins is on firmer ground.

KEITH: Let's take a quick break, and we will be back with more in a moment.

And we're back. And, Ximena, you've been doing some really interesting reporting about how immigration is playing out in the midterms so far. And you went through a bunch of ads that have run in various congressional races. What did you find?

BUSTILLO: Yeah. So essentially, according to data that has been gathered by the firm AdImpact, Republicans, starting in January of this year through June, have spent way more money and ran way more ads related to immigration than Democrats. And this analysis includes ads that are exclusively about immigration or immigration enforcement or border security, and that's all they talk about. It also includes ads where, you know, a candidate will laundry list items like healthcare, housing, the border, you know, inflation, like, the next thing. And so that gets counted in this analysis as well because it is one of items that candidates want to talk about.

KEITH: Yeah, I mean, one of the ads I watched, I don't even know if they mentioned the word immigration, but the shot that ended the ad had the candidate standing in front of President Trump's border wall.

BUSTILLO: Exactly, a lot of border security, a lot of imagery, and a lot of connections to various issues. And Republicans, in their advertising, really saw this as a way to connect between, you know, what the Trump administration has essentially given them, a slate of various policies to campaign on from, you know, going after alleged noncitizen voting to limiting birthright citizenship to securing the border, which is a very basic, you know, campaign point that has been a winner for Republicans. And then, Democrats primarily did focus on enforcement and kind of the recent funding that has gone to the agency.

KEITH: All right. Well, let's hear a few of these ads.

(SOUNDBITE OF MONTAGE)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: A massive operation.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Agents came with their guns drawn.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #3: A series of ICE raids took place today.

MICHAEL BENNET: Donald Trump's war on immigrants is an attack on all our fundamental rights. I'm Michael Bennett.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #4: Nebraska needs a voice brave enough to take on Trump and his ICE thugs. Denise Powell, daughter of Cuban and Chilean immigrants.

KEVIN STEELE: I'm Kevin Steele, and I approve this message.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #5: Socialists, radicals, open border extremists - they're coming back, and they're coming for our president.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #6: She's going to fight in Congress for you, to deport criminal aliens and lower our cost of living.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: This is a fantastic woman - Laurie Buckhout.

KEITH: And I guess it probably goes without saying, but the first two ads were from Democrats and the second two ads were from Republicans.

BUSTILLO: And, you know, the data collected by AdImpact does show that both of these issues are, you know, in the top three for both Republicans and Democrats. No. 1 issue - Donald Trump, right? Like, Donald Trump is obviously the No. 1 issue. People are either running for him or against him. And then, you know, immigration as a word is No. 2 for Republicans. And then for Democrats, you get healthcare, and then you get ICE.

KEITH: Wow. And Mar, I find this really interesting that Republicans are talking about immigration so much because in a way, the story coming from President Trump is that all of the problems of immigration that existed before he was president, they have been solved. The border is closed. People aren't coming in. The message that Trump and Republicans have so effectively used in previous elections, like, there are caravans coming or the borders are open, now they can say, we solved that.

LIASSON: They can, but that's not as motivating as a message that scares people, like you just heard in that ad. You know, our candidate is going to deport criminal aliens. The problem for the Republicans is this messaging works pretty well in primaries when you're trying to motivate the base to vote for you and show that you're the hardest-line hard-liner on immigration. But the question is whether this is going to work for them in a general election. Because what we've seen with the immigration issue is it used to be Trump's No. 1 issue, polled very well, especially when the focus was on border security and deporting undocumented immigrants with criminal records. People were for that. But then when the discussion became about shootings of U.S. citizens, of undocumented workers who didn't have a criminal record or were on their way to work or had been part of communities for 25, 30 years, then those numbers on immigration began to drop and his immigration agenda became unpopular, like almost every other part of his agenda.

So for a general election, especially in the small number of truly competitive districts, immigration might not work as well for Republicans in a general election. But right now we're in primary season, and they are using the kind of same messaging about immigrants inundating our country, causing prices to go up. That's a message that has worked for them in the past. The big question is - and we'll be watching this, obviously - is it going to work when we switch to the general election?

KEITH: Right. And Ximena, your analysis was largely focused on primaries.

BUSTILLO: Yes. Oh, pretty much. You know, since we are about halfway through the primary season, nearly all the ads are about primaries. There are a few Senate races where, you know, you saw some Republicans already talking about the Democrat - thinking Alaska, thinking Ohio. But for the most part, it's Democrats running against Democrats, Republicans running against Republicans on, like, each other's records on the issue.

LIASSON: Although, Maine - you know, you have to put Maine in there. Maine is a special race, the only blue state in the country where there's a Republican Senate incumbent up for reelection. And it also just happens to be a state where we had one of these ICE killings recently.

KEITH: And I think it's important to explain - and, like, I think we can't say this too many times - there are not very many competitive races come November, which means that in so many districts, the primary is the election. That messaging is the messaging that gets that person into Congress. In fact, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, there are only 18 house races that are true toss ups out of 435 that are on the ballot. Ximena, what about Democrats? How is their messaging in these ads? What did you see?

BUSTILLO: Yeah, so a lot of it, kind of, as I alluded to earlier, was a lot more focused on enforcement tactics, overreach there. You know, some ads even go as far as to say, we support deporting people with criminal records, but that's not what this administration is doing. And then a lot of personal stories, a lot of leaning on someone's personal immigration story or of their parents or of someone in their community.

KEITH: And how many Democrats are talking about eliminating ICE?

BUSTILLO: Not as many as you might think. So it is a message that does still exist, and we've seen this primarily in states like Illinois, Minnesota and Colorado and a few of the Dem-competitive races in New York. And so some Dems were really going after members of their own party, especially, you know, the first three states that I mentioned did see waves of target of ICE enforcement, you know? And so I think a lot of that really pushed more progressive candidates to lean into that message. But by and large, it not the unifying message of the Democratic Party.

But I think generally on the issue of immigration, that is where having a unified message can be a really big challenge for entire parties, because the way that immigration affects a border community or affects an urban area or affects a rural community can be completely different. And so both Democrats and Republicans are going to grapple with this, you know, instinct to, I think, have a unifying tagline. But that unifying tagline is probably not going to win you every single race, and it might lose you some races.

LIASSON: You know, I have to push back on this. They don't need a unifying tagline. They're being told, run your own race. They don't need a national tagline on this issue. You're going to have diversity because every time we have a midterm, the Democratic Party says, run your own race. There's no national policy on these issues. And just - we've got to throw Maine in here again because Maine is a race where there is a Democrat, Troy Jackson, and he is an abolish ICE guy, and he has staked out a position that's not necessarily going to be super popular in a general election. But I don't think there's pressure on Democrats to adhere to a national position on abolishing ICE. I don't.

KEITH: Yeah, I don't think that Ximena was saying that either.

LIASSON: Oh, oh.

BUSTILLO: I was saying what you were saying, Mara. I was saying, like, in fact, there probably is pressure for them to not say that.

KEITH: Yeah.

BUSTILLO: Like, there is probably more pressure for them to not say, abolish ICE and to say something like reform...

LIASSON: Oh, I thought you said they were looking for a message that would be, like, an overall unifying message for all Democrats.

BUSTILLO: I mean, yes, but the unifying message wouldn't be abolish - like, OK. So there is an instinct for political parties to have a unifying message on policy issues.

LIASSON: Oh, see, that's where you and I disagree. Yeah. That's where we could disagree. OK.

BUSTILLO: But whether or not it is abolish ICE - it is probably not abolish ICE. More candidates, they're going to turn to the lessons of 2018 when they did do that, and it did not work for them. But there are some progressives in states like Minnesota, Illinois, Colorado that saw increased enforcement that are pushing that envelope and are breaking with the mold.

KEITH: I can't wait for you to come back and talk to us about their general election messaging in a couple of months and see where this lands. We're going to leave it there for today. I'm Tamara Keith. I cover politics.

BUSTILLO: I'm Ximena Bustillo, and I cover immigration policy.

LIASSON: And I'm Mara Liasson, senior national political correspondent.

KEITH: And thank you for listening to the NPR POLITICS PODCAST.

text:
SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- A local leader who caught video of ICE agents arresting a Ukrainian woman at San Francisco International Airport is speaking out.

"I'm waiting for my flight, waiting for my group to be called. And her - a woman - screaming for help on top of her lungs," said Richmond City Councilmember Doria Robinson. "Any you know, just every lady alarm went off, like there's somebody who needs help."

Richmond City Councilmember Doria Robinson was there watching the event unfold.

"Just all of us - hundreds of people at all of our gates - watching this thing happen. That just was a thing that shouldn't happen, " she said.

VIDEO: Video shows ICE agents in plain clothes detaining Ukrainian woman at SFO

Iryna Gorb was taken into custody Wednesday after returning from a trip to Portland, according to friends and state Sen. Scott Wiener, who has helped connect her with legal assistance.

The arrest gained widespread attention after Robinson recorded video of the encounter at SFO. The footage, which quickly circulated online, shows agents detaining Gorb inside the airport.

"This is just another example of ICE going over the top," Wiener said. "This is a woman who has committed no crime. And remember Trump promised he was going after the worst of the worst violent criminals."

Friends say Gorb, a Ukrainian national, has built her life in San Francisco, working in cafes and as a photographer. They describe her as a longtime member of the city's community and say they were shocked by her detention.

"She's lived in San Francisco for a decade; she works here; she has friends here; she's part of our community, and they just grabbed her and want to deport her back to a war zone," Wiener said.

The senator, who has authored several state laws aimed at protecting immigrant communities, also criticized ICE's tactics. Wiener noted that agents involved in the arrest appeared to be in plain clothes, a practice that has drawn scrutiny in recent immigration enforcement operations.

"Why they feel the need to roam around SFO is beyond me," Wiener said. "They are not doing anything to keep the community safe; they are just engaging in a torture campaign, a terror campaign."

In a statement to ABC7 Eyewitness News, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed Gorb's arrest and defended the agency's actions.

"Gorb overstayed her visa and remained in the United States illegally for 15 years in violation of our nation's laws," the statement said. "She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceeding."

Friends have been working to secure legal representation and track Gorb's whereabouts as she moves through the immigration detention system.

Andy Eblin, a close friend, said he spoke with Gorb after her arrest and described her as increasingly distressed.

"She is substantially more rattled than the last time I spoke with her, given she's been pulled halfway across the state and put in a detention facility," Eblin said.

Eblin said the video recorded by Robinson proved critical in helping friends understand what had happened.

"That video has been incredibly, incredibly instrumental," he said. "We'd be in a much, much worse situation without it."

As attorneys prepare to challenge her detention, Gorb remains in ICE custody awaiting immigration proceedings. Her case comes amid ongoing debate over federal immigration enforcement and the administration's policies toward undocumented immigrants living in the U.S.

text:
A federal appeals court won’t stay an order overturning the $100,000 Trump fee on new H-1B workers hired from outside the US.

The government hasn’t shown it’s likely to succeed in challenging a district court’s decision that the fee exceeded the president’s authority, a panel for the US Court for the Appeals for the First Circuit said in an order Friday.

A federal judge in Boston ruled June 8 that the fee violated the US Constitution’s separation of powers by exercising the exclusive tax authority of Congress, handing a win to the Democratic states that sued over the policy.

Judge Leo Sorokin of the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts later agreed to grant a request by the Trump administration to pause his order until the First Circuit weighed in on the administration’s request for an emergency stay.

The Department of Justice said in court filings that the government is likely to succeed with claims that the fee is a justified use of the president’s foreign commerce and immigration powers. Additionally, Sorokin’s order prevented Trump from addressing national security concerns connected to the H-1B visa program, DOJ argued.

Decisions on separate challenges to the fee are pending at the US District Court for the Northern District of California and the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. —

Federal officials on Friday are drawing attention to the case of a Sacramento County man accused of sexually assaulting a child while he was a daycare worker.

Previous coverage in the video player above

A news release from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement filed a detainer request asking for Gokhan Bagci, a Turkish national, to remain in custody. A detainer request is a call to keep a person in custody and for officials to cooperate with ICE before the person is released.

The Sacramento County Sheriff's Office said in 2025 that Bagci was working at the Mather Childcare Center, which primarily serves members of the Turkish community. Deputies began investigating after a mother reported that she believed her daughter had been sexually abused.

While interviewing the child, the sheriff's office said investigators came to believe other children might have been sexually abused. Detectives then arrested Bagci on Aug. 22, 2025, on charges of lewd and lascivious acts with a child under 14 by force of fear.

DHS said the child's mother reported that Bagci "lured the girl into a closet pretending to play hide-and-seek, where he sexually assaulted her."

"He then allegedly brought the girl into a bathroom and raped her that same day," DHS said.

Bagci had been removed from the country by the U.S. Customs and Border Protection in November 2023 and again in September 2024, the sheriff's office previously stated.

Jail records show his next court appearance is set for 8:30 a.m. on July 31.

KCRA 3 reached out to the sheriff's office for comment. Below is the agency's response.

"In accordance with the Truth Act, we would honor the detainer after a felony conviction. At this point, the individual has been charged but has yet to be convicted. This request is premature on their part."

text:
A case asking whether the Trump administration can build a border wall across tribal land in Arizona appeared in court for the first time this week.

President Donald Trump’s first administration built a 30-foot steel bollard wall across just over 450 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border. Some 230 miles of it were in Arizona, but the roughly 60-mile long stretch of border inside the Tohono O’odham Nation was not included.

That’s changing now, as the administration plans another border wall along vast stretches of public land — and inside the tribal nation.

The tribe filed suit this year to try and stop it. Congresswoman Adelita Grijalva, whose district includes the Tohono O’odham Nation, says the plan risks destroying important cultural sites.

“This administration is willing and continuously violating tribal sovereignty, and threatening all of these culturally and environmentally significant lands,” she said. “And once you have disrupted the land, there is no way to put it back together.”

This week in a Washington, D.C., district court, attorneys for the tribe argued that wall plans disregard sovereign Tohono O’odham boundaries — which can only be changed by Congress. The government argues the 60-foot stretch of land where the wall would be built is under federal control.

text:
WASHINGTON (MNTV) — An American Civil Liberties Union report alleges widespread civil rights violations, excessive force, and misconduct in immigration enforcement across eight states during the second Trump administration.

The report examined more than 1,200 incidents involving federal, state, and local agencies in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Louisiana, Maryland, and New Mexico between January and December 2025. It documented more than 50 deaths in ICE detention and at least eight additional fatal shootings by ICE and Customs and Border Protection officers.

Use of force runs through the findings. The ACLU identified 375 incidents involving physical force or its threat — pushing, tackling, restraint, weapons — including dozens using tactics civil rights experts warn can restrict breathing or cause serious injury.

It also flagged vehicle-related practices, with agents alleged to have boxed in cars, forced dangerous driving, and struck vehicles or people, echoing the “he used the car as a weapon” accounts that have followed multiple ICE killings this year.

Children recur throughout. The report documents 157 cases involving children during operations near schools, at traffic stops, in home raids, and at check-ins, including at least 54 in which agents directly questioned or detained a child.

Nor were the targets only undocumented: the ACLU logged 200 incidents involving US citizens, lawful permanent residents, and people protected under DACA who were allegedly detained or targeted, along with cases involving people with disabilities, older adults, and pregnant women.

In one, two Honduran women detained at Louisiana check-ins were deported with their children, including US citizen children — one child, the report says, with a rare cancer, removed without medication or any handoff to doctors.

The numbers are the argument. Fifty deaths in detention and a child with cancer deported without her medicine are not the byproduct of a system straining under scale; they are what the system is producing, and the ACLU’s call for oversight, accountability, and safeguards is a request that someone be answerable for it.
