text:
Oregon and 25 other states are suing the federal government over new grant conditions.

The lawsuit claims the Trump administration is attaching unrelated immigration and election policy requirements to public safety funds.

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield has joined a coalition of 26 states and the District of Columbia in a federal lawsuit filed in Rhode Island against the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Department of Homeland Security to block new conditions attached to hundreds of millions of dollars in grants from those agencies.

“The Trump Administration is playing politics with people’s lives and with the safety of our communities,” said Rayfield in a statement. “Oregonians know firsthand what it takes to recover from wildfires, floods, and ice storms – we don’t need the federal government using natural disasters or terrorist threats to score political points.”

An unnamed FEMA spokesperson referred to the lawsuit as a “partisan pushback."

"We fully expected these left-wing politicians to oppose common-sense measures designed to protect election security and safeguard the integrity of American democracy," the spokesperson wrote.

The lawsuit takes aim at new conditions to the Homeland Security Grant Program, which was established after the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, under the USA PATRIOT Act.

Oregon was allocated $4,362,750 in State Homeland Security Program grants and $5,539,967 for the Urban Area Security Initiative in the 2026 fiscal year. Oregon was allocated another $5,033,692 under the Emergency Management Performance Grant Program.

The states have been allocated over $740 million in Fiscal Year 2026 HSGP funds that now include conditions unrelated to public safety, the complaint said. Billions of dollars are affected nationwide.

According to the complaint, the Trump administration announced new requirements for the FEMA Homeland Security Grant Program that require recipients to overhaul how they run elections and enforce immigration law to fit Trump administration election policy.

The complaint references a revised notice of funding opportunity issued on July 9.

The notice had what the states characterize as "generally applicable terms and conditions" that FEMA intends to impose on the HSGP grant program, but also included five “National Priority Areas” for states to address in their grant applications. The notice directs that 30% of funding awarded to a state must be allocated to projects addressing those priority areas. One such priority area relates to enhancing election security.

Grantees would be required to make “at least one investment" that supports physical and/or cyber election security, and applicants are required to allocate at least 3% of the SHSP and UASI award to such investments, according to the court filing. And there would also be five additional requirements:

Verify voter citizenship using DHS’ U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements or SAVE database.

Verify the citizenship of election workers using the SAVE database.

Transition away from voting systems using QR codes or bar codes to count votes to equipment that accepts hand-marked paper ballots.

Conduct post-election audits under DHS guidelines

And reconcile voter and ballot counts using DHS-set methodology.

The updated notice and a guidance issued by DHS on July 9 also stated that FEMA will withhold 20% of the recipient’s total HSGP award until the recipient submits proof of compliance with the election security requirements.

The complaint also takes aim at DHS, including a set of conditions in its 2026 fiscal year standard conditions requiring states to assist the federal government in enforcing federal civil immigration law.

Those conditions have been titled “Communication and Cooperation with the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration Officials" which include: not restricting government entities or officials from exchanging information with DHS concerning the citizenship or immigration status of any individual, complying with criminal laws that prohibit "inducing" noncitizens to unlawfully enter the country, honoring requests for cooperation, providing federal immigration agents with access to detainees in correctional facilities, and not publicizing any federal immigration enforcement operations.

"Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump Administration," the FEMA spokesperson said. "Concerns over voting processes, data security, and registration practices have made it clear that action is required. This year, states must take critical, common-sense steps to protect U.S. elections before receiving their full Homeland Security Grant Program awards. These new requirements will preserve election integrity.”

Rayfield won similar lawsuits in 2025, also in Rhode Island federal court.

The filing argues that the federal administration is trying to achieve what courts have already blocked.

"Since January 2025, defendants have engaged in a concerted campaign to use the grant programs administered by DHS and FEMA to force States and local governments to adopt the current Administration’s preferred policies," the complaint said.

Rayfield joined the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin, and the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania in the lawsuit.

title: Attacks on human dignity can never be normalized, say 2 US bishops after deadly ICE shootings
description:
(OSV News) -- Two U.S. Catholic bishops are lamenting recent deadly immigration enforcement encounters, calling for God-given human dignity to be respected in every individual.
On July 14, ICE agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian, after being stopped by ICE agents near a laundromat.
The Trump administration briefly halted, then resumed, ICE traffic stops in the wake of the deaths.
"Our pastoral concerns are distinct from what the civil law itself may permit," said the two bishops.
In a report released in June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights counted 52 deaths in ICE custody during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration.
text:
(OSV News) -- Two U.S. Catholic bishops are lamenting recent deadly immigration enforcement encounters, calling for God-given human dignity to be respected in every individual.

"As Catholics, we believe that all persons are created in the image and likeness of God and, therefore, grieve all situations where human life is brought to an unnatural end. This is a core teaching of our faith and one we can never grow weary of proclaiming as disciples of Our Lord Jesus Christ," said Bishop Daniel E. Garcia of Austin, Texas, and Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Victoria, Texas.

The two issued a July 20 joint pastoral reflection as chairs, respectively, of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Subcommittee for the Promotion of Racial Justice and Reconciliation and the USCCB's Committee on Migration.

Their statement follows three separate deaths recorded days apart in July amid operations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers as they implement the Trump administration's hardline crackdown on immigration.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Houston area man, was fatally shot en route to work in his vehicle July 7 during an ICE traffic stop. On July 14, ICE agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian, after being stopped by ICE agents near a laundromat. Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, a 28-year-old man from Mexico, was struck and killed by a tractor trailer July 15 in St. Augustine, Florida, while fleeing ICE and Homeland Security agents on foot.

ICE's claims that Salgado and Durán attempted to ram officials with their respective vehicles have been disputed, with Houston law enforcement officials expressing frustration over the federal agency's lack of collaboration in investigating forensic evidence in Salgado's death.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that Salgado -- a Mexican national who had been in the U.S. for some 35 years, and who was in the process of obtaining legal authorization to reside and work in the country -- was not the intended target of the ICE operation in which he died.

In Colorado, an employee of the GEO Group -- a private firm that contracts with ICE to operate its Aurora processing center -- opened fire July 16 on a protester at the site, injuring the woman's foot.

The Trump administration briefly halted, then resumed, ICE traffic stops in the wake of the deaths.

In their statement, Bishops Garcia and Cahill quoted from the USCCB's November 2025 special pastoral message on immigration: "We are disturbed when we see among our people a climate of fear and anxiety around questions of profiling and immigration enforcement."

Drawing on the USCCB's 2018 pastoral letter on racism, "Open Wide Our Hearts," the bishops stressed that "racial profiling in particular violates God-given dignity," adding the practice "also inflicts profound harm on individuals, families, and communities by fostering fear, eroding trust, and increasing the risk of unjust and even tragic outcomes. "

"Our pastoral concerns are distinct from what the civil law itself may permit," said the two bishops.

They warned that "acts that diminish or disregard the dignity of any person or group of people should never be normalized in our society," pointing to both "the dehumanization of immigrants, regardless of their legal status" and "the vilification of law enforcement officers" as examples.

Bishops Garcia and Cahill said they "continue to affirm the legitimate role of civil authorities to implement the law in a humane manner and with respect for fundamental human rights, including the rights to life and due process."

Underscoring that "the power of the state must always be exercised within the limits of the moral law," they called for "accountability, transparency, and justice, which require that meaningful reforms be made to our immigration system."

The bishops said they "join in praying for the souls of those killed and for their families, for our nation, and for all those entrusted with the duties of public service."

They also prayed "for an end to dehumanizing rhetoric, racial prejudice, and violence and for a renewed commitment to recognizing the inherent dignity of every person as a child of God," and pleaded for "the intercession of Mary, Our Mother, who is the model of perfect faith in times of grief, hardship, and uncertainty."

According to data analyzed by The Guardian, eight persons -- including U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti -- have been shot to death by federal immigration agents under the current Trump administration as of July 15, with 13 injured and another 9 other shooting incidents with no injuries.

In a report released in June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights counted 52 deaths in ICE custody during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration. The two organizations said ICE "fails to disclose adequate information about the circumstances surrounding deaths in its custody," with medical neglect suspected as a key factor.

As of April, more than 60,000 are in ICE custody, the majority of whom (just under 71%) have no criminal convictions, according to Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Gary Peters (D-MI), Ranking Member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, is demanding an explanation for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) purchase and use of a powerful commercial spyware tool capable of accessing cell phone messages, photos, location data, microphones, and cameras without a user’s knowledge. In a letter to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Peters pressed for documents and information detailing how Paragon Solutions’ Graphite technology is being used, the legal authorities governing its deployment, and what safeguards are in place to protect Americans’ privacy and civil liberties.

“Graphite is a powerful, invasive cyber tool, the procurement and use of which represents one of the most significant expansions of DHS and ICE’s surveillance ambitions to date and creates significant risks to the national security of the United States,” Peters wrote. “Graphite, like other spyware tools, silently breaches devices to exfiltrate messages, photos, files, location data, and other saved data while also activating microphones and cameras – turning personal devices into surveillance tools without the user’s knowledge.”

Authoritarian governments around the world have used the same Graphite spyware tool to target journalists, human rights advocates, opposition politicians, and other members of civil society. Although ICE has confirmed it possesses the technology, the agency has declined to answer key congressional oversight questions about who may be targeted, whether the spyware has been deployed domestically, or what legal authorities govern its use.

“Given concerns about ICE’s collection of information about Americans, including about First Amendment-protected activities such as protesting and social media posting, and immigration enforcement officers’ references to ‘nice little databases,’ I am deeply troubled about how Graphite might be used in the United States to target Americans,” Peters wrote.

During consideration of Republicans’ June budget reconciliation bill, Peters pushed for a vote on an amendment to the legislation that would have prohibited DHS from using spyware like Graphite on United States citizens. Republicans unanimously voted down the proposal.

The Cedar Rapids Police Department released new video from the July 7 arrests outside a Homeland Security Investigation (HSI) office in southwest Cedar Rapids, saying it provides broader context for an officer's use of force that was captured in a widely shared social media video.

The video posted earlier this month show police slamming Annya Mari to the ground. She was charged with interfering with official acts and harassment of public officials.

New Surveillance/Bodycam video:

The video was released Thursday as police continues its review the incident, which occurred outside the federal facility at 3351 Square D Drive SW.

According to police, officers were dispatched at about 12:26 p.m. after federal officials reported people were trespassing, blocking government vehicles from leaving the property and interfering with federal employees attempting to exit the facility.

Police said that at the request of federal officials, an officer contacted those involved.

In the newly released video, you can see the protestors place themselves very close to moving government vehicles, spitting on cars and make obscene gestures.

During the interaction, police say Scott Boylen ran from the officer and was later arrested on a charge of interference with official acts.

text:
A group of 25 Democratic attorneys general led by California’s Rob Bonta are taking the Trump administration to court for imposing “unlawful” conditions on federal grants for disaster preparedness and response.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) have been placing stipulations on federal grants that amount to a “campaign of coercion” designed to force states to adopt the White House’s preferred voting and immigration policies says the lawsuit, filed in federal court in Rhode Island on Thursday.

Those requirements, which have been imposed on more than $740m in combined funding for disaster preparedness and counter-terrorism, include mandating states employ a federal system to verify the citizenship of all voters and conduct post-election audits.

The lawsuit also targets agencies’ attempt to withhold funds to states who do not agree to assist Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in conducting raids and deportations – a mandate that a federal court struck down last year. And it calls out a new condition giving Fema the ability to cancel state grants if they are found to be out of alignment with the agency’s priorities.

“President Trump has little support for both his mass deportation agenda and his baseless claims of election fraud, so instead, he’s trying to bully state and local governments into adopting his preferred policies in exchange for much-needed funding,” Bonta said in a statement.

Reached for comment, a Fema spokesperson called the lawsuit “partisan pushback” against “commonsense measures” from “leftwing politicians”.

“Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump Administration,” the spokesperson said. “These new requirements will preserve election integrity.”

Bonta and other Democratic attorneys general have previously filed two successful challenges over the same grant programs. In a ruling affirming the second of those lawsuits, a Trump-appointed judge wrote: “To hold hostage funding for programs like these based solely on what appear to be Defendants’ political whims is unconscionable and, at least here, unlawful.”

The DHS and Fema were apparently “undeterred” by their previous losses, says the Thursday lawsuit.

“The administration has already lost similar fights in court, and we expect this latest unlawful attempt to fail as well,” Bonta said. “Our communities deserve better than to have essential resources caught up in political games.”

Washington — The ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee is demanding that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement explain why it has purchased commercial spyware capable of covertly taking control of phones as well as collecting messages, photographs, location information and other personal data.

Democratic Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan called the purchase "one of the most significant expansions of DHS and ICE's surveillance ambitions to date," flagging potential civil liberties concerns and risks to U.S. national security. Peters sought clarity from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a letter exclusively obtained by CBS News and dated July 23, calling into question ICE's $2 million, sole-source purchase of Graphite, a surveillance tool developed by Paragon Solutions and now owned by REDLattice.

"Misuse of Graphite is not hypothetical," Peters wrote, mentioning public reporting that more than 90 journalists and civil society members were targeted by the technology across several countries.

While the senator from Michigan does not allege that ICE has used Graphite against journalists, protesters or other Americans, Peters demanded the agency disclose whether the software has been deployed domestically, who has been targeted and legal authority supporting use of the tool.

The ranking member said he was "deeply troubled about how Graphite might be used in the United States to target Americans," pointing to ongoing concerns about ICE's collection of information involving protests, social media posts and other First Amendment-protected activities.

Peters also asked ICE for the number of U.S. and non-U.S. people who have been targeted, where they were located and why the software was procured. He also requested information about whether the data collected by Graphite has been shared with other government agencies, companies or nonprofit organizations.

The lengthy inquiry seeks contracts, privacy assessments, civil rights reviews, security policies and records connected to a September 2024 agreement, an October 2024 stop-work order and the contract's later reactivation in August 2025.

In his letter, Peters said his committee staff had requested briefings from the Department of Homeland Security in December 2025 and from ICE in January 2026, but never heard back substantively.

The ranking member requested an immediate briefing and gave ICE until Aug. 7 to provide documents and answer questions about the spyware's use, oversight and security. text:
A Catholic nun who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers while walking to Mass in South Texas said that she continues to live with fear and uncertainty weeks after her arrest drew national attention and bipartisan calls for her release.

Sister Leticia “Letty” Ugboaja, a 56-year-old nun from Nigeria, spoke publicly for the first time since she was detained by ICE officers on June 28 in McAllen, a city just north of the U.S.-Mexico border. During a news conference July 23, Ugboaja described being stopped by two armed federal officers as she walked to Our Lady of Sorrows Church for Sunday Mass, where she was scheduled to serve as a eucharistic minister.

“I was very much afraid, with cold sweat,” Ugboaja said at the news conference. “I did not expect on an ordinary Sunday morning when people should be ready to go to Mass to worship the Lord" that she would be taken into custody.

Ugboaja was released later the same day after intervention from members of Texas’ congressional delegation and public outcry over the detention of a nun wearing her habit on her way to worship. The case sparked criticism from both Democrats and Republicans, who questioned why she had been detained.

Ugboaja said many other immigrants face similar situations without the public attention her case received. She urged immigration authorities to give people an opportunity to be heard before they are taken into custody.

"There are many others in this same situation, people who have been given some form of protection under our laws, who have followed every rule asked of them, and who still live with uncertainty," Ugboaja said.

USA TODAY has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and ICE for comment.

Attorney says nun remains protected from deportation to Nigeria

Ugboaja's attorney, Carlos M. Garcia, said an immigration judge denied Ugboaja's asylum claim in 2019 but granted her protection from removal to Nigeria, concluding that "she had met the high legal standard required to show it was more likely than not that she would face torture if returned there."

That protection bars the U.S. government from deporting her to Nigeria, Garcia said, though she remains under a final order of removal because her asylum application was denied. Ugboaja has complied with all conditions of her immigration status since the ruling, including maintaining employment authorization and attending required immigration appointments, according to Garcia.

“She has done everything the law has asked of her,” he said at the news conference.

Ugboaja is scheduled to report to ICE on July 28, and Garcia urged federal authorities not to detain her again or require her to wear an electronic monitoring device.

When Ugboaja was detained last month, Garcia said she was given little explanation for why she was being taken into custody. He noted that ICE was attempting to remove her to a third country.

Over the last year, the Trump administration has dramatically expanded a little-known tactic of sending migrants to countries where they have no ties, USA TODAY previously reported. Critics have said this outsources detention to foreign governments − often those with records of human rights abuses, minimal oversight and unclear legal protections.

In more than two dozen countries, deportees have been held in hotels, shelters and prisons under agreements brokered by the United States during President Donald Trump's second term.

Nun's detention prompted public outrage

Ugboaja's detention quickly drew national attention after church leaders, immigrant rights advocates and Texas lawmakers rallied on her behalf. Daniel E. Flores, the bishop of the Catholic Diocese of Brownsville, described her as a "well-known source of goodness and hope" in the community.

Ugboaja is part of the Daughters of Mary Mother of Mercy congregation, which is headquartered in Nigeria, according to the diocese. She volunteers as an Extraordinary Minister of Holy Communion at Our Lady of Sorrows Church and is a registered nurse at South Texas Health System's McAllen Medical Center.

Before volunteering at the church, Ugboaja worked for a decade as a certified nursing assistant at DHR Health in Edinburg, Texas, the diocese said in a statement following her detention.

As news of Ugboaja's detention spread, Rep. Monica de la Cruz, a Republican, and Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar, Vicente Gonzalez and Joaquin Castro were among the lawmakers who criticized the incident and pressed federal officials for her release.

The League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), the oldest and largest Latino civil rights organization in the United States, also launched a petition calling for an immediate investigation into Ugboaja's detention.

De la Cruz, Cuellar, Gonzalez and Castro have intervened in other immigration cases that sparked public outrage. In March, Castro and de la Cruz announced that two teenage brothers − who were part of an award-winning mariachi band − and their parents had been released from ICE custody.

Contributing: Eduardo Cuevas and Jennifer Borresen, USA TODAY

title: ICE is detaining more people in Wisconsin jails. Immigration attorneys are scrambling to keep up.
description:
ICE is detaining more and more people in Wisconsin jails — and most of the people detained have no criminal convictions.
Congress requires the Department of Homeland Security to release data on immigration detention every two weeks.
According to the analysis, the average number of people in detention in Wisconsin on a given day hovered around 115 between 2023 and 2025.
RF: Many arrested by ICE in Wisconsin are detained out-of-state.
RF: The network of Wisconsin jails cooperating to hold ICE detainees is expanding.
text:
ICE is detaining more and more people in Wisconsin jails — and most of the people detained have no criminal convictions.

That’s according to a Milwaukee Journal Sentinel analysis of detention data that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released this week. Congress requires the Department of Homeland Security to release data on immigration detention every two weeks. But this is the first time they’ve done so in months.

According to the analysis, the average number of people in detention in Wisconsin on a given day hovered around 115 between 2023 and 2025. But in 2026, that number rose to 147 — a 25 percent increase.

According to the data, 54 percent of those people have no criminal convictions. Last year, that number was higher, at 75 percent.

As a partner at Eastbridge Law Group in Madison and legal director at the Community Immigration Law Center, Aissa Olivarez has helped clients navigate detention and file petitions to be released. She joined WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” to talk about what these recent developments look like for the people being arrested and detained.

The following interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Rob Ferrett: When someone is detained, what happens with their immigration proceedings?

Aissa Olivarez: Many people that we are seeing detained are in the middle of their proceedings and have done everything they’re supposed to. They’ve checked in with ICE, they’ve been monitored on an alternative to detention, and they’ve submitted their applications.

But they find themselves now in a detention facility with proceedings being expedited, possibly not having access to their lawyer in the same way they did when they were not detained, and now they need to get together crucial evidence that’s going to determine their case in just a couple of weeks.

RF: Many arrested by ICE in Wisconsin are detained out-of-state. Does that create additional hurdles as people seek to be represented either for a bond hearing or for their ongoing immigration proceedings?

AO: We are seeing people from Wisconsin transferred outside of the jurisdiction in Kansas, Kentucky and Indiana. It means that they’re farther from family and oftentimes from their lawyer and the conditions vary across all of these facilities.

But some of these facilities are outside of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit and might have favorable case law around a bond hearing, and so what we’re seeing is that we’re able to move more swiftly and more quickly toward reunification of a family if they’re transferred outside of the 7th Circuit.

RF: When someone is detained — especially out of state — how do you find them?

AO: It can be difficult. Sometimes it takes days to find somebody. Oftentimes, we’re getting this information from family members because people are given a phone call, and they’re able to advise about where they’re being taken to or where they might be transferred to. So we really rely heavily on our families for this type of information, so that we can locate people before they’re inside officially of the system, and try and schedule a confidential phone call, so that we can speak with them about what their rights are in that facility.

RF: The network of Wisconsin jails cooperating to hold ICE detainees is expanding. Is it sometimes better for someone to be detained in a Wisconsin facility, closer to home?

AO: Of course, there’s a benefit to being close to counsel and close to nonprofits that are doing the work. But unfortunately, I think any cooperation with ICE and jail space means increased detention and really facilitates increased arrests that we’re seeing here in Wisconsin.

I believe capacity might come into their discretion on whether or not to arrest, because there is a lot of discretion involved on the side of ICE. We’re seeing now how many more people don’t have criminal convictions, how many more people are being held in the state of Wisconsin, and I think it’s this cooperation that allows for that expansion.

Rob Ferrett: How long does it usually take to file a federal habeas corpus petition — a petition to challenge their detention in front of a judge?

AO: We do a quick assessment about whether they would be bond eligible if they were given a bond hearing. … If they’re eligible, we do proceed with that federal habeas corpus petition, but we’re up against the clock. The immigration judges are under a lot of pressure from the Department of Justice to move forward very swiftly with people’s removal, and so oftentimes we’re not getting decisions on these federal court petitions and able to get somebody released before there’s a decision on their case.

RF: In a situation where someone has been arrested and detained by ICE, what kind of things should be the first actions that they or their family members should take?

AO: It’s important for people to have discussions with their family about what this could look like. Oftentimes, you are able to ask ICE questions, to make a phone call, to ask them where you’re being taken to, so that you can share these details with your family. You’re given a case number right away. That case number helps lawyers to find out where you are in the posture of your proceedings and get important information to determine whether or not you might be bond eligible.

RF: Legally, does due process in the U.S. apply to people who are not citizens?

AO: Due process is part of the constitution, and the constitution covers people regardless of their immigration status. It protects us from the arbitrary exercise of power by the government. And unfortunately, the mass detention and deportation agenda has significantly escalated the lack of due process for people because they are placed into an expedited proceeding, they are in detention and it can be really difficult to access legal representation.

At a bare minimum, people facing deportation should be able to understand the proceeding against them in a language that they understand, alongside somebody who understands immigration law. Due process is an essential safeguard to our country’s fundamental democratic values as we work to advance immigration policies that respect fairness, family unity and human dignity.

text:
A British-born man who has lived in the US since he was nine years old has been held in an ICE detention facility for more than a month and a half under threat of deportation, it has been reported.

Connor Read, 29, was taken by ICE agents after he was invited to a green card (residency permit) interview in Tampa, Florida on 3 June, and separated from his wife, Jaelin, 25, and his twin sons Ryder and Ozzie, three.

Originally from Chatham in Kent, Read was brought to the US in 2007 as a child by his mother and stepfather. He attended American schools and only returned to the UK once.

According to the Times newspaper, he was subject to a removal order in 2011 but at the age of 16 was granted Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (Daca) status, a policy that provides deportation relief and work permits to eligible individuals brought to the US as children.

But while afforded the Daca protection, Read reportedly committed minor offences that led to him being deemed a “criminal illegal alien” by the Trump administration, including convictions for possession of narcotic equipment, possession of liquor and resisting an officer.

The Times reports that because of the narcotic charge, at the age of 22, Read was unable to renew his Daca status. He met Jaelin on a dating app in 2020, when his immigration status was unsettled. Having married, the couple attempted to apply for a green card.

On 3 June, Read was invited to attend a green card meeting at the federal immigration building in Tampa. In the interview room, four ICE agents arrested him and removed him from the building. Immigration officials told Jaelin Read that her husband would not be coming home.

He was taken to Pinellas county jail in Florida, where he spent eight days in a shared cell and was later flown to an ICE detention centre in Louisiana. He is appealing against his final removal order but has been warned a decision may not come for up to six months.

An ICE spokesperson told the Times: “Connor Michael Read, a criminal illegal alien of the United Kingdom, was arrested on 3 June 2026 by the ICE law enforcement in Tampa, Florida.

“His criminal history includes convictions for possession of narcotic equipment, possession of liquor and resisting an officer. He was issued a final order of removal issued by an Orlando, Florida immigration judge from January 2011.

“Read entered the United States on 21 November 2007, through the Orlando international airport as a non-immigrant with an F-2 visa, as a dependent of an F-1 non-immigrant student. Read’s status was contingent upon his parent’s status as a student. After a violation of the terms of their visa, Read was placed into removal proceedings.

“Under President Trump and [homeland security] secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the US.”

text:
A federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to redetain a Georgetown University scholar who was arrested by ICE last year as part of the administration’s campaign to crack down on foreign nationals who expressed pro-Palestinian views.

Badar Khan Suri, an Indian postdoctoral fellow at the university who is married to a US citizen, was arrested in March 2025 and detained for nearly six weeks at a Texas detention center before a federal court ordered him released on bail. The fourth circuit court’s decision on Thursday upheld that ruling and rejected the government’s attempt to move the case from Virginia to Texas.

The 2-1 decision is a win for individuals in immigration custody who seek to challenge their detention through the federal courts system and by invoking the constitutional principle of “habeas corpus”, which allows all individuals detained by the government to challenge their detention in court.

The ruling follows two earlier ones by other appeals courts considering similar cases that reached the opposite conclusion, teeing up a likely supreme court decision on the matter. In January, a different decision ruled in favor of the government in a similar appeal brought against former Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil. And earlier this week, a third appeals court reached the same conclusion in a ruling against Mohsen Mahdawi, another Palestinian student at Columbia whom the government also detained last year.

In those cases, the judges reviewing the appeals sided with the government’s position that the judges who ordered Khalil and Mahdawi’s releases had overstepped their authority by intervening before the cases had moved fully through the immigration court system – a process the Trump administration controls through the Department of Justice and which critics have long denounced as political.

Immigration cases can take months or years to resolve, and those rulings would effectively make it impossible for those held in immigration detention to seek redress in federal court. Khalil’s lawyers have said they will seek review from the supreme court; a decision in his case will have implications for Khan Suri, Mahdawi and other detained immigrants seeking intervention from federal courts.

Addressing the court’s decision in Khalil’s case, the panel of judges reviewing Suri’s plainly stated: “We disagree.” They called that reading of the law “absurd”.

“[In] our view,” the court wrote, “denying judicial review of detention claims like Suri’s misreads Congress’ statutes and undermines the protections guaranteed all persons on American soil by the writ of habeas corpus.

“If a noncitizen is challenging their detention pending removal, then waiting for their removal proceedings does them no good,” the panel added, noting that such a position would make cases in which immigration detention is wielded in unconstitutional ways “effectively unreviewable”.

The justice department and Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond for a request for comment.

Noor Zafar, a senior staff attorney with the American Civili Liberties Union’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, hailed the appeals court decision. “The federal government cannot do an end run around the first amendment by locking people up for their speech and denying them their day in court,” she said in a statement. “Immigration laws cannot be abused to silence dissent.”

Suri was targeted by the administration over his social media criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza, including concern he expressed for his Palestinian-American wife’s family there.

In a statement, he said that the appeals court’s ruling reaffirmed “that an independent judiciary remains the truest guardian of liberty, due process, and the rule of law”.

text:
A woman whose arrest by plainclothes ICE agents at San Francisco International Airport was captured on video has been identified by friends as a 38-year-old Ukrainian who has lived in San Francisco for more than a decade.

Iryna Gorb begged for help and said agents were choking her as she sat on the floor during her arrest on Wednesday at the airport in the widely viewed Instagram footage (opens in new tab).

“Please help me,” Gorb, a photographer and cafe worker, said as a crowd formed around her. “Let me go.”

Gorb was returning to the city from a trip to Portland, according to her friend Andy Eblin. He spoke to her later that night when she called from a facility in Stockton, he said. He spoke to her again briefly on Thursday evening after she’d been transferred to a detention facility in California City.

“This is a story about Iryna, but it’s a bigger story about the lack of humanity,” Eblin said. “It’s horrendous,” he said about the footage.

She sounded “shaken” by the ordeal, he said.

Her immigration status had been a source of anxiety for her, as had ongoing worries about the war in Ukraine, said Eblin. She had begun seeing a therapist to deal with the stress.

”It was really a huge driver of anxiety for her,” he said. “She would always try to change the subject,” if someone mentioned it.

A group of friends rallied in her defense to find a lawyer to represent her and raise money on GoFundMe (opens in new tab). Her parents left Ukraine after Russia invaded and now live in Slovakia, he said.

“She doesn’t have immediate family here, but she does have family,” Eblin said about the circle of friends who are devastated by her arrest. “She’s fiercely loyal, always willing to help friends, tough, [has] strong opinions, but is incredibly kind and caring.”

State Sen. Scott Wiener offered to connect her with legal services and offered advice to her friends on locating her. In a statement, he condemned her arrest.

“ICE’s terror campaign against our communities must end. Iryna Gorb made a home in San Francisco and is one of many people who help make San Francisco run,” Wiener said. “She is part of our community. Iryna committed no crime, but ICE nevertheless violently grabbed her and is now trying to deport her to Ukraine, a war zone currently being invaded and bombed by Putin.”

The viral video of Gorb’s confrontation was posted by Richmond city councilmember Doria Robinson. She did not respond to The Standard’s inquiries.

The San Francisco Police Department spokesperson Evan Sernoffsky said the “SFPD was not involved.” The department had been criticized in March after officers were seen creating a barrier between ICE agents arresting a Guatemalan woman with her daughter, and a crowd of travelers who watched in the airport terminal.

An SFO spokesperson said airport officials only knew about the incident from social media posts.

“ICE and DHS are federal agencies that operate outside the jurisdiction of U.S. airports, including SFO,” said Doug Yakel by email. “As a result, we are not involved in any decisions about their operations, nor are we notified when they occur.”

text:
Video showing a Ukrainian woman being arrested by immigration agents at San Francisco International Airport on Wednesday is drawing attention and raising questions about how the arrest was carried out. This comes alongside a spike in similar stories around the country since June, a trend that has attorneys cautioning their clients not to fly.

Video taken of this incident shows a woman in a white shirt and dark pants on the ground outside a store inside SFO, while two men -- who appear to be dressed in plainclothes -- pin her to the floor.

The woman shouts out, "You're choking me!" and "Please help me!" as people gather around and ask the men what they are arresting her for.

At one point, the woman shouts out, "I'm from Ukraine!"

Doria Robinson, who happens to be a city council member for the city of Richmond, was in the airport just before 7:45 p.m. that evening. She was waiting to board her flight at the time and recorded video of the incident, which has since been shared by many different accounts across social media.

Robinson said she was inside the Harvey Milk Terminal at the B7 gate, already past security, when she heard "a woman screaming at the top of her lungs."

"I looked across, and I saw two men taking a woman who was in a shop across the way, pulling her down to the ground, getting on top of her as she’s screaming," Robinson recalled.

Initially, she said she wondered if it was a domestic violence incident or human trafficking. But as Robinson walked towards the commotion, she realized something else was going on and began recording with her phone. Robinson estimated that hundreds of people around the terminal were also watching this unfold.

Robinson said that she did not see the two men wearing any clothing or identification showing who they worked for. Also, she said, despite questions from the crowd about who they were with, the men refused to answer. Ultimately, she said the men handcuffed the woman and carted her away in a wheelchair.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed to NBC Bay Area that on July 22, ICE arrested a Ukrainian woman named Iryna Gorb at SFO. The spokesperson added that when officers approached Gorb, "she attempted to flee and resisted arrest."

DHS said Gorb lawfully entered the U.S. in 2010 on a visa that allowed her to stay in the country until the end of May of 2011. DHS said Gorb overstayed her visa and stayed in the U.S. for 15 more years.

"She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings," the DHS spokesperson said.

Several immigration attorneys told NBC Bay Area they had seen the video of this arrest on social media.

"You could hear the fear and the pain in the woman’s voice," said Bay Area immigration attorney Ghassan Shamieh.

Shamieh does not represent Gorb, but said the video was chilling for him to watch. He said that he and other immigration attorneys in his circle have noticed a spike in detentions at airports in the past few weeks.

Shamieh said four of his clients have been detained in airports, including one last week at SFO. He added that of his clients who have been detained at airports, none of them have criminal records.

"That’s why advocates and immigration attorneys alike are advising clients not to travel via plane even domestically within the United States," Shamieh said.

As for Robinson, she said she is disturbed by this arrest and wonders what will happen to Gorb.

"What we do know is we were complicit in it, and there was nothing we could do to help her, and that was just demoralizing, just painful," Robinson said.

A spokesperson for SFO told NBC Bay Area Thursday that the airport doesn't have any details about this incident "apart from what we've seen on social media."

The spokesperson noted that ICE and DHS are federal agencies operating outside the jurisdiction of U.S. airports.

"As a result, we are not involved in any decisions about their operations, nor are we notified when they occur," the spokesperson continued.
