text:
Washington Attorney General Nick Brown and a coalition of states sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Federal Emergency Management Agency today, arguing the agencies are unlawfully attaching political conditions to billions of dollars in federal counterterrorism and emergency preparedness funding.

The lawsuit challenges FEMA and DHS decisions to impose new requirements on federal funds Congress appropriated to help states prepare for and respond to emergencies and natural disasters, including acts of terrorism. The coalition argues the conditions would coerce states into changing how they conduct elections and into assisting DHS with enforcing federal immigration law.

SEE ALSO | FEMA opens federal disaster aid for Washington after December storms and flooding

“Funding to protect Washingtonians from terrorism and catastrophe should not be subject to politics,” Brown said. “It’s the third time we’ve been forced to take these agencies to court to follow the law as Congress intended.”

According to the lawsuit, DHS and FEMA have established grant conditions for 2026 funding that affect billions of dollars, including more than $1 billion in Homeland Security Grant Program funding used by states to support security measures and protect residents from terrorism, cyberattacks and other threats. In recent years, Washington has received about $20 million in HSGP funding each year.

The coalition says the agencies are again threatening to impose immigration-related conditions similar to those attempted in 2025 across federal grant programs. Those conditions were found unlawful and blocked by a district judge last year, the lawsuit states.

The attorneys general also argue DHS and FEMA are threatening to withhold 20% of each state’s counterterrorism funding unless states change election laws to align with what the coalition calls an unlawful federal effort to control voting.

The lawsuit says the requirements would force states to abandon years of work and millions of dollars invested in election security systems in order to receive unrelated funding Congress earmarked for preventing terrorist attacks.

The challenged conditions include requiring states to conduct a mandatory 5% manual audit of voting systems, reconcile voters and ballots using a methodology DHS has not disclosed, and use DHS’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system to verify the citizenship of every election worker and every registered voter in state voter databases.

The lawsuit says DHS and FEMA would withhold at least 20% of each state’s HSGP funding for noncompliance.

The coalition also challenges a condition that would allow FEMA to terminate any grant program “for any reason,” arguing it would create a constant threat of termination that undermines how the programs function. The notes say a federal court recently rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to interpret an existing regulation in a similar way.

The attorneys general argue the grant conditions violate the Administrative Procedure Act and the U.S. Constitution’s Spending Clause.

Joining Brown in filing the lawsuit are the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Wisconsin, along with the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.

text:
A U.S. General Services Administration lease for a Southfield office being used by the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor, ICE’s legal wing, has drawn protest and criticism from the surrounding community since plans were first reported in February. At a panel hosted on Wednesday night, community organizers gathered to emphasize the importance of neighborhood solidarity in the face of ICE activity in the region.

Lauren Fink, who, along with her husband Cameron, started the Southfield Neighbors Action Committee in response to the news of the Southfield office, told the crowd that, following news that a proposed detention facility in Romulus would be sold by ICE, resistance to the agency’s presence in Southfield remains important — and the win in Romulus shows that they can be pushed out.

“People need to be just as disgusted by what is happening in REDICO building at One Towne Square as they are by the idea of a detention center in Romulus, and we should be just as disgusted by what is happening in that office building, because it is disgusting,” Fink said, referring to the building owners. “What is happening in that office building is what enables these detention centers.”

The event, titled “What Does It Mean to Be a Good Neighbor When ICE Moves In?” focused on how the local community can react and respond to immigration enforcement.

Beyond the regular protests hosted by Fink and her colleagues, panelists emphasized the need to support the broader community — especially those at risk of becoming targets of ICE themselves.

Elida Reyes founded Community Action for Empowerment, or CAFE, to advocate for immigrants in Oakland County and to provide direct support for those most impacted — volunteers document arrests, deliver food to affected families, and transport them to court appointments.

At Wednesday’s event, she told the story of Vera, a young Venezuelan immigrant who arrived in Pontiac knowing no one, having fled the regime of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Reyes took her in after she came to her church looking for a place to stay.

“I treated her as if she was my granddaughter, and I put her through the school,” Reyes said. “And no one can say she didn’t have papers because we paid for the attorney. We made sure she had all her papers.”

But after leaving Michigan to visit a friend in Florida, she was stopped by ICE, detained in Louisiana, and was eventually deported to Venezuela — and Reyes has not been able to reach her since earthquakes devastated the country in June.

She has continued her work through CAFE, accompanying people to court hearings and doctor’s appointments where they fear they or their loved ones might be detained by ICE.

“I started this a year ago,” Reyes said. “I’d like to end it, but we can’t until it’s done.”

She further urged those in the room to similarly look out for their neighbors, offering support in times of need.

“I’ve got grandkids, and I don’t want them to go through this. I’ve got grandkids, and I worry about their future every single day,” she said. “I don’t know what our future looks like, but if we don’t change it, it’s not good. It’s really not good.”

Dr. Patricia Talley, attending the panel as part of the Afro-Mexican advocacy organization Mexico Negro, A.C., similarly emphasized the need for community support in the face of ICE’s presence in Michigan.

“We are all good neighbors,” she said. “We want to live in a beloved community, one where everyone is respecting their basic humanity.”

Talley’s mother, Barbara Talley, was a trailblazer for the civil rights movement in Michigan — she was the first Black member of Southfield’s city council, first elected in 1983. Throughout the event, she referenced the King Center’s work on nonviolence to inspire the community response to immigration enforcement — contacting elected officials, telling stories of immigrants, and attending town halls like the one held on Wednesday.

“We’ve been so culturalized to accept these things,” she added. “We become complacent.”

REDICO, which owns the One Towne Square building with the GSA lease in question, was invited to participate in the panel, according to organizers — a seat was reserved for the company’s CEO, Dale Watchowski.

Asked why Watchowski did not attend, Fink said, “We sent them an invitation. We would love to have conversations with them. We have had conversations with REDICO in private. We have attempted many times to have conversations with REDICO in public. It has not been successful. I think the answer is because they don’t want to be here.”

A statement from REDICO said that Watchowski “was out of town traveling on business and has no record of receiving an invitation to this meeting.”

The statement continued on to say that REDICO has engaged consistently with local officials and community members on the GSA lease.

“The terms of the lease explicitly prohibit any law enforcement, detention or similar activities from occurring at the property,” the statement continued. “REDICO is prepared to fully enforce the agreement if the terms of the lease are violated. We have been observing the usage closely. REDICO cannot unilaterally cancel a legally binding lease with the GSA, or any tenant, unless the terms of the lease are in default. To date, government usage of the space has been for office purposes only, which is well within the terms of the lease.”

U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit), whose district includes Southfield, also spoke at the event remotely.

“When ICE comes into one community and violates people’s civil rights or uses weapons, excessive force, it is a violation of all of our civil rights,” she said. “These are real human beings, real lives that are being impacted, but it’s being done in a very dehumanizing, very aggressive way that it really doesn’t create a fair, just immigration system.”

Emphasizing local organizations working to provide support and legal representation to those facing immigration detention, Tlaib also emphasized her concerns about federal law enforcement activity on Election Day — and how those are directly tied to the current immigration enforcement regime.

“You all think about ways you can obviously uplift and show what ICE is doing with the billions of dollars that the Trump administration has been pouring in there,” she said. “It’s important to understand the impact of what the Trump administration is doing, using these law enforcement agencies or these extensions of agencies that are supposed to be keeping us safe. They’re actually not doing that.”

text:
Jesús Manuel Arenas-Silva was at home in Georgia with his family on July 9 when Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents came to arrest him. Sonimar Maria, Arenas-Silva’s sister, said her family implored the agents not to take the 45-year-old Venezuelan, mentioning his medical needs, but ICE did not listen to their pleas.

Flanked by progressive House Democrats and speaking in Spanish to reporters at a Capitol Hill press conference on July 22, Sonimar said ICE agents also ignored her family’s request to let Arenas-Silva take his medication with him. Arenas-Silva required four different medications for a medical condition, Sonimar said, but ICE allowed him to bring only one to the remote Irwin County Detention Center in rural Georgia.

“Jesús Manuel later told me on a phone call that ICE did not give him the medication he needed,” Sonimar said in a translated statement. “He went without medication during his detention until he tragically died in ICE custody on July 13 … I am 100 percent certain that he did not receive proper care.”

Arenas-Silva died while being transferred from Irwin County Detention Center to the Folkston ICE Processing Center, a roughly 100-mile drive. He was found unresponsive five days after he was arrested, according to ICE. At least 53 people have died in ICE custody since President Donald Trump returned to office and launched a mass deportation campaign led by adviser Stephen Miller, making the past fiscal year the deadliest in the agency’s history.

Additionally, at least 30 people have been shot in public or in their homes by federal immigration agents during Trump’s chaotic crackdown, and 11 have died, including multiple parents and two United States citizens. Sonimar is calling for an independent investigation into her brother’s death, but the Trump administration has consistently erected barriers to accountability for both the deadly shootings and the deaths in ICE jails.

“He was a loving son, brother, and uncle, a caring and hard-working man who came to this country to seek better opportunities,” Sonimar said of Arenas-Silva, adding that she came to Washington, D.C. to seek justice for her brother so that other families do not have to endure similar trauma.

Some Democrats are pushing for structural changes to put an end to the violence enacted by ICE, which has been emboldened under policies set by Trump and Miller. At a House Judiciary Oversight Subcommittee hearing on conditions in ICE jails on July 22, Democrats slammed the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress for spending billions of dollars to build immigrant jails and recruit poorly trained federal immigration agents while slashing funding for health care and food assistance.

Progressive House Democrats are going a step further than simply questioning ICE’s tactics and bloated budget. They propose abolishing the agency altogether and redirecting its funding to safety-net programs that can help people navigate a spiraling affordability crisis.

“Americans are demanding members of Congress pursue more than training, more than reform, and more than bare-minimum policies,” said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Illinois) a July 22 press conference. “They are demanding that no other family suffers the pain of deportation or death at the hands of DHS’s immigration enforcement.”

In January, Ramirez introduced H.R. 7190, or the Melt ICE Act, which would dismantle ICE by ending the Department of Homeland Security’s authority to surveil and jail immigrants. The legislation would also redirect enforcement funding toward federal housing and health care programs that recently suffered budget cuts under Trump and the GOP, as well as groups that support migrants and households with noncitizen family members.

“ICE agents are murdering people in the streets, tearing families apart, abducting our neighbors, and locking them in cages,” said Rep. Rashida Tlaib, a Democrat from Michigan and co-sponsor of the bill. “ICE must be abolished — full stop. The billions of dollars that funded ICE should be given to the communities who suffered under their reign of terror.”

In the past month alone, ICE agents shot and killed two unarmed fathers in their vehicles while they were driving to work: Immigration agents killed Joan Sebastian Guerrero on July 13 in Maine and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo on July 7 in Texas. Both men were reportedly not initial targets for arrest and were pursued by Trump’s immigration officers in vehicle stops in what civil rights activists suspect are clear-cut cases of racial profiling. Guerrero, a husband and father of a 3-year-old, was reportedly killed by an ICE agent who was recently recruited despite a well-documented history of violence and abuse.

On July 22, Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán was fatally struck by a semi-truck in Florida while fleeing ICE agents. Coronilla Durán had a tourist visa and was visiting family in the U.S. while on vacation from Mexico. An advocacy group assisting Coronilla Durán’s wife said she thought “he was very afraid, and that’s why he ran away.” Ramirez echoed that, adding Coronilla Durán likely ran away out of fear of being arrested and detained in one of ICE’s notorious jails and prison camps, where people are dying at a record rate.

“He did what my brother would have done, he did what your sister would do, he did what your mother would do if she was stopped by ICE and looked a certain way — he ran away,” Ramirez said. “He was afraid they would take him to a private detention center where he could die in days and never see his family ever again.”

A recent ramp-up of enforcement is impacting citizens and noncitizens alike as recently deputized and heavily armed federal agents raid homes and target random people on the street to increase Trump’s deportation numbers. A review of 1,200 incidents involving ICE and its partners by the American Civil Liberties Union found the tactics being deployed are causing civil rights violations at a “scale and severity without precedent in our nation’s recent history.”

Ramirez reminded fellow lawmakers that Congress created ICE and the Department of Homeland Security only 25 years ago following the 9/11 attacks and can be dismantled just the same.

“I know that people are saying, ‘You are radical, you want to melt ICE’; people are asking, ‘What is going to happen with detention?’” Ramirez said. “I say to people: Look at our history, and we had a Department of Justice that handled all of our immigration cases until 2003, and I want to remind people that people were not dying the way they are dying right now.”

So far, only 13 Democrats have co-sponsored Ramirez’s Melt ICE Act: Tlaib, along with Representatives Yvette Clarke (New York), Ilhan Omar (Minnesota) Yassamin Ansari (Arizona), Nydia Velázquez (New York), Adelita Grijalva (Arizona), Jesús G. “Chuy” García (Illinois), Valerie Foushee (North Carolina), Ayanna Pressley (Massachusetts), Summer Lee (Pennsylvania), Danny Davis (Illinois), LaMonica McIver (New Jersey), and Sylvia Garcia (Texas). Ramirez suggested that most of the signatories are people of color.

“To all of our white allies in Congress, this is the moment to join the movement to melt ICE,” Ramirez said. “I want to see your last names here, too.”

The Melt ICE Act has virtually zero chance of passing while the GOP holds a majority, but the bill represents an important political Rubicon for Democrats as their base pushes for change in the midterms.

As the elections approach in November, Republicans are deploying a familiar strategy of casting Democrats as radical “communists” who want to defund law enforcement. In reality, the party’s establishment has consistently provided plenty of funding for police, including in the years following the nationwide outbreak of protests against racist police violence in 2020 that called for defunding police.

Republicans painted the entirety of the Democratic Party as supporters of the “abolish ICE” and “defund the police” movements anyway, and establishment figures and pundits often mention those movements in their discussion of their electoral losses in 2024. However, Republicans are now on the back foot. Trump is deeply unpopular, with his approval ratings on the economy and immigration plummeting since taking office.

A YouGov poll released on July 21 found that about half of all U.S. adults now support abolishing ICE, including 73 percent of Democrats. Only 40 percent somewhat or strongly oppose eliminating the agency. News of ICE killings appears to be reaching voters, with 60 percent telling pollsters they heard about ICE shooting and killing people in the last week.

In a July 21 letter to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, more than 100 progressive state lawmakers, city council members, and politicos from his home state of New York demanded that Democrats in Congress come out in support of abolishing ICE. After Joan Sebastian Guerrero was killed by ICE in Maine, the debate over abolishing ICE became central to a much-watched Senate campaign in the state, with Democratic hopeful Troy Jackson recently confirming that he supports dismantling the agency.

Maine Gov. Janet Mills, a moderate Democrat, wrote in a July 15 letter to the state’s congressional delegation that the “violence has to end” before more gunshots shatter a windshield and another family loses a loved one. “ICE needs to be fundamentally reformed, and if not, then it is time to abolish it,” Mills wrote.

As Ramirez pitched the Melt ICE Act again this week, a coalition of immigrant rights groups launched End the ICE Age, a campaign to dismantle ICE as an agency and pressure Democrats to co-sponsor the Melt ICE Act.

“People are dying in ICE detention at a record-breaking rate, ICE agents are tearing families apart and shooting people on the streets, making people less safe, and causing chaos wherever they go — whether in Minneapolis, Chicago, Los Angeles, Houston, Biddeford, or beyond,” said Setareh Ghandehari, advocacy director at Detention Watch Network. “Make no mistake, we are witnessing a watershed moment.”

text:
A federal judge has ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to release a man who was arrested outside a Baltimore school in June, rebuking the tactics used by agents during the arrest.

Jesus Acevedo Sanchez and his partner, Adriana Gavilan Sanchez, were taken into custody by ICE agents while dropping off their daughter at Commodore John Rodgers Elementary/Middle School on June 11.

Judge Julie Rubin ordered immigration officers on Thursday to release Acevedo Sanchez from the Farmville Detention Facility in Virginia by midnight. But as of early Friday morning, he was still listed in ICE custody.

In court, Judge Rubin said this case is a "stomach churner" and that ICE did not have probable cause to arrest Acevedo Sanchez outside of the school. Rubin added that ICE officers did not follow the procedures put in place for due process.

"His immediate release is the proper and only remedy," she said.

Caught on camera

CBS News Baltimore obtained video showing ICE agents detaining the two, as a window was shattered on their vehicle.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told CBS News Baltimore last month that Acevedo Sanchez "refused lawful commands, violently resisted arrest, and used his vehicle to evade law enforcement, dragging an ICE officer in the process."

DHS also initially alleged his partner Gavilan Sanchez punched officers, but later in an affidavit wrote there was "minimal physical resistance."

Last week, a judge ordered ICE to release Gavilan Sanchez.

"As our brave law enforcement arrests and removes dangerous criminal illegal aliens, including murderers, rapists, and gang members from our communities, America can be proud of the professionalism our officers bring the job day-in and day-out," a spokesperson for DHS said in a statement Friday morning. "Since Day One, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump's promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S. More than 3 million illegal aliens are out of the country. We will continue to deliver on the President's promise to make America safe again."

How arrest unfolded

The couple was driving in their SUV with their children just after 7 a.m. when they noticed someone following them as they pulled out of a Dunkin' Donuts, according to their attorneys.

The unmarked vehicle with ICE officers inside then tried to pull the SUV over at Dundalk Avenue and O'Donnell Street.

They cut off his vehicle and slammed on their brakes; then, men wearing all black got out yelling with guns drawn and one broke his driver's side window, Acevedo Sanchez's attorney, Rachael Savage, told Judge Rubin.

"He was terrified it was a random act of violence," Savage said. Her client then drove to his daughter's school "seeking protection."

Savage said her client was not questioned until he was placed in the ICE holding facility in downtown Baltimore. She said at the time of his detention, there were no removal proceedings against him.

"They had no probable cause; he was in the U.S. illegally. They had no probable cause to stop him," Savage said.

Her co-counsel Rachel Girod told the judge, "He thought he was fleeing a carjacker who was coming for him and his elementary school-age daughters."

She said Acevedo Sanchez went to their school because he knew there would be police officers present.

"He was trying to get his daughters to safety," Girod said.

In an interview with WJZ-TV Investigator Mike Hellgren, Girod said, "Wouldn't anybody [think they were being carjacked]? A man jumps out wearing all black head to toe, breaks your window, and points a gun at you and your little girls in the back seat. You're going to do whatever you can to protect your family and that's what he did, and the judge saw it for what it was."

Government responds in court

Assistant U.S. Attorney Beatrice Thomas told Judge Rubin the stop was justified. She said it was a "targeted enforcement operation" and ICE was trying to determine if Acevedo Sanchez was in the country illegally.

Thomas said ICE ran checks on Acevedo Sanchez that turned up nothing and wanted to question him. She said that's why ICE ordered Acevedo Sanchez to get out of the car.

"He did not comply. He decided to drive over a median, knocking over our officer," Thomas told the court. She also claimed the ICE officers "were in fact in uniforms" and insisted they "did have the authority to arrest this person."

She did not provide specific information when the judge asked what initially led ICE to believe Acevedo Sanchez was in the country illegally. In her ruling, Judge Rubin noted Acevedo Sanchez entered the United States illegally in 2007 from Mexico. She said he had no criminal record. His daughters are U.S. citizens.

Judge criticizes ICE

Judge Rubin said the government's arguments were not persuasive.

She found the ICE officers initially "did not wear any item that identified themselves" and believed Acevedo Sanchez's account that he thought he was a victim of a carjacking, including that he thought a bullet had pierced his window when the ICE officer broke it with his weapon.

"Out of fear they were going to kill him and his family, he jumped the median to get away when the officer was knocked to the ground," she read from her ruling in court.

Judge Rubin said the lack of a warrant gave ICE more limited authority, and she was critical of the officers for not immediately identifying themselves and providing Acevedo Sanchez a reason for the arrest. She said the arrest was a "violation of the framework in place to afford due process."

Judge Rubin told the courtroom, "His arrest and detention are not justified."

She also said the lack of records when police searched Acevedo Sanchez's name in computer databases was no reason to pull him over.

"It is unclear how a negative hit leads them to believe a person is in the U.S. unlawfully," Judge Rubin said. She noted a search of her own name would not lead to a "hit" in the system and said there would be no reason for ICE to stop her vehicle.

Girod told WJZ she was grateful for the judge's tough language against the immigration enforcement efforts in this case.

"I think we especially need to consider that language because she said that was her being restrained," she told Hellgren.

She and Savage said they were leaving court to tell Acevedo Sanchez and his partner the news about the release and then make arrangements to bring him back to Maryland.

"They are very much at the front of our minds, and our emotional reaction to the decision was all about them," Girod said. "We're excited to share that with them and get back to work so we can do that."

Baltimore City Council hearing

As Acevedo Sanchez's court hearing was underway, members of Baltimore's City Council were holding a hearing on the impact of immigration enforcement on school grounds, which was prompted by his arrest, believed to be the first by ICE on a public school campus in Maryland.

"We are seeing our community, the Latino community, the immigrant community attacked every day," said Odette Ramos, who represents the city's 14th District. "No one deserves to be in that situation."

Ramos said the city is doing everything it can to protect the immigrant community and an arrest at a school was "unacceptable."

"Every student who is supporting another student is impacted — all of our families who are seeing these tragedies happen every single day — and we have to take a stand and be brave and show that we will not accept this," Ramos said. "This is not normal, and attacking one community because of how they speak, because of how they look, is just not acceptable."

text:
(Washington, D.C.) – Today, U.S. Representative Emanuel Cleaver, II (D-MO), reintroduced the Transportation for Reentry Act, legislation designed to help formerly incarcerated individuals successfully reintegrate into their communities by expanding access to reliable, affordable public transportation during the critical first year after their release.

Each year, approximately 610,000 Americans leave state and federal prisons. While many are eager to find work, attend medical appointments, reunite with family, and rebuild their lives, the cost and availability of transportation often stand in the way.

“Too often, we tell returning citizens to get a job, keep appointments, support their families, and contribute to their communities, while denying them one of the most basic tools needed to accomplish those goals: a reliable way to get there,” said Congressman Cleaver. “If we are serious about reducing recidivism, strengthening public safety, and helping people rebuild productive lives, we must remove unnecessary barriers to success. The Transportation for Reentry Act is a practical investment in second chances, safer communities, and a stronger workforce.”

"Every person deserves an opportunity to rebuild their life after incarceration, but a lack of transportation to work or a probation meeting can derail their progress. Transportation should never determine whether someone succeeds or is pulled back into the criminal legal system. Rep. Cleaver's Transportation for Reentry Act recognizes that safety means investing in the tools people need to thrive in their communities. Federal programs that remove re-entry barriers and promote economic opportunity are smart justice investments in people, not prisons,” said Nina Patel, ACLU Justice Policy & Government Affairs Senior Policy Counsel.

The Transportation for Reentry Act would expand the Federal Public Transportation Program to provide eligible individuals recently released from incarceration with up to one year of free public transportation, helping connect them to employment opportunities, education, healthcare, substance use treatment, housing resources, and other critical community services.

Specifically, the legislation would:

Establish a new Public Transportation Reentry Service, funded at $40 million annually from FY2027 through FY2031, to provide free transit services for eligible returning citizens

Authorize the U.S. Department of Transportation to reimburse participating transit agencies, provide technical assistance, and promote awareness of the program

Direct public transit agencies to establish localized enrollment and service systems for returning citizens

Require a Government Accountability Office evaluation of the program’s implementation and effectiveness to inform future improvements

Research consistently shows that stable employment, housing, and access to community resources significantly reduce the likelihood that formerly incarcerated individuals will reoffend. Reliable transportation is often the first step toward achieving each of those goals.

The Transportation for Reentry Act is cosponsored by Reps. Wesley Bell (D-MO), André Carson (D-IN), Troy Carter (D-LA), Judy Chu (D-CA), Jasmine Crockett (D-TX), Dwight Evans (D-PA), Valerie Foushee (D-NC), Maxwell Frost (D-FL), Robert Garcia (D-CA), Glenn Ivey (D-MD), Jonathan Jackson (D-IL), Pramila Jayapal (D-WA), Hank Johnson (D-GA), Jan Schakowsky (D-IL), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-NJ), and Frederica Wilson (D-FL).

The Transportation for Reentry Act is endorsed by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), Ella Baker Center for Human Rights, Prison Policy Initiative, Tzedek Association, Voice of the Experienced (VOTE), and the Formerly Incarcerated, Convicted People and Families Movement (FICPFM).

View full bill text here.

Emanuel Cleaver, II is the U.S. Representative for Missouri's Fifth Congressional District, which includes Kansas City, Independence, Lee's Summit, Raytown, Grandview, Sugar Creek, Greenwood, Blue Springs, North Kansas City, Gladstone, and Claycomo. He is a member of the exclusive House Financial Services Committee and Ranking Member of the House Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance.

text:
A Dallas-based flight attendants union is standing behind one of its members after a Southwest Airlines employee was taken into ICE custody last week.

Federal officials say Lorenzo Thompson overstayed his visa, but supporters say there is more to the story.

“I was shocked,” said Edward Marq, member of the Labor Council for Latin American Advancement.

Marq says he couldn't believe the news, then learned the flight attendant detained last week wasn't just a coworker; he was a fellow member of TWU Local 556, the Dallas-based union of Southwest Airlines flight attendants.

“He is a union brother to me,” Marq said.

Marq is also a flight attendant for Southwest Airlines.

Marq says Lorenzo "Enzo" Thompson was detained by ICE on July 14, after returning to Nashville International Airport from a work trip.

“Enzo came to America from Jamaica in 2021, he applied for and received a workers permit, so he applied to work with Southwest Airlines and he’s been with us all this time,” Marq explained.

Marq says Thompson has a pending asylum case.

The Department of Homeland Security told NBC 5, “ICE ERO New Orleans officers arrested Lorenzo Thompson, an illegal alien from Jamaica, at Nashville International Airport.Thompson entered the United States lawfully on April 17, 2021, at the Miami Port of Entry, with permission to stay for six months. Thompson never departed and remained in the U.S. illegally for five years in violation of the terms of his lawful admission.

Thompson was cooperative with ICE officers and taken into custody without incident. Cooperation of this nature helps ensure the process is conducted safely and efficiently for all involved. He will remain in ICE custody pending immigration proceedings.”

Marq said, “People describe Enzo as very loving, as very caring, very friendly, everyone that he has flown with has really enjoyed their flying and it is evident by the outpouring of support that I have seen on social media.”

Thompson's family and friends declined to discuss details of the case saying they don’t want to jeopardize the legal process, but thanked people for prayers, donations and support. Thompson's union says it’s also working with Thompson's family, his attorney and its own legal counsel.

“We’re worried about him, but it’s beyond an immigration case. It’s about a worker, it’s about a union member, it’s about a family. Everyone deserves that due process and to have their case heard fairly,” Marq said.

Online records show Thompson is being held at a correctional center in Mississippi.

Southwest Airlines has not responded to NBC 5’s request for comment.

title: ICE nears 600,000 deportations since Trump took office - Washington Times
description:
All told, since President Trump took office in January 2025, ICE has tallied nearly 600,000 removals and more than 500,000 book-ins, which are proxies for arrests.
Mr. Mullin took office vowing to avoid all that while still trying to deliver on President Trump’s mass deportations.
TRAC doubted that 2,000 arrests were realistic over the long term.
The latest ICE data show that, as of July 11, 63% of those in custody had either convictions or pending charges, according to ICE’s own statistics.
The new ICE data is the first update the agency has published since April.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is hitting its deportation stride under Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, executing an average of about 1,250 formal removals a day over the past three months, according to agency data.

That is down from the peak in removals at the start of this year, when the Department of Homeland Security flooded cities with high-profile street-level sweeps. Still, it is much higher than under the Biden administration and, for the most part, has been accomplished with fewer headlines than those that plagued Mr. Mullin’s predecessor, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, whom Mr. Trump fired.

“I’ve turned down the temperature of the stove to get it correct, without boiling over,” the secretary told reporters last week.

All told, since President Trump took office in January 2025, ICE has tallied nearly 600,000 removals and more than 500,000 book-ins, which are proxies for arrests.

In recent months, ICE has averaged 1,150 book-ins a day, according to the new data. That is still less than the January peak, when the agency was conducting high-profile operations in major cities, but it is significantly higher than ICE managed in February and March, after the city surges ended.

ICE reported 65,765 migrants in detention as of July 11, up from about 60,000 in April but down from a high of more than 70,000 in late January.

Those January highs came with big downsides, including massive resistance protests in Minneapolis and Chicago, streets choked with federal government tear gas, news coverage of parents and children being snared in arrests, and the shooting deaths of two U.S. citizens during confrontations with federal immigration agents in Minneapolis.

Mr. Mullin took office vowing to avoid all that while still trying to deliver on President Trump’s mass deportations. For the most part, that has been true, though the calm was shattered earlier this month by the shooting deaths of two immigrants during confrontations involving ICE agents in Texas and Maine. Both incidents remain under investigation.

Administration officials say recent weeks have set new records for arrests and deportations.

Mr. Mullin told reporters they were setting “single-day records, every single day.”

The New York Times reported that ICE considers 2,000 daily arrests the new standard.

The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, which tracks Department of Homeland Security enforcement numbers, said ICE averaged 1,474 arrests a day in the first 11 days of July. TRAC doubted that 2,000 arrests were realistic over the long term.

“While these temporary surges can generate headlines, ICE has not in the past demonstrated the ability to sustain them,” the organization said.

The department declined an invitation to provide specific numbers to The Washington Times but hailed the work of the government’s deportation agency.

“ICE is NOT slowing down,” the department said in a statement.

Mr. Mullin said 70% of those ICE is arresting “are felons, or have pending felony charges.”

White House border czar Tom Homan, in an interview with the Center for Immigration Studies, put the figure at 60%.

The latest ICE data show that, as of July 11, 63% of those in custody had either convictions or pending charges, according to ICE’s own statistics.

That was up from 56% during the early-year surge.

Mr. Homan said the arrest numbers are high despite major headwinds, including sanctuary cities and federal judges who have ordered migrants released and blocked deportations, questioning the legality of ICE operations and tactics.

He said he is “happy” with the numbers, but not “satisfied.”

“We need more arrests, and we need more deportations,” he told the center.

He also said he is still pushing to reach 100,000 detention beds.

The new ICE data is the first update the agency has published since April.

It used to be produced every couple of weeks, but the department said the partial shutdown that followed Democrats’ blocking of the department’s spending bill in an attempt to force changes to ICE policy left the agency unable to finalize the data.

title: Criminal – Immigration consequences – Plea - Massachusetts Lawyers Weekly
description:
… “The defendant argues that the advice he received regarding the immigration consequences of his plea was constitutionally deficient.
“To be sure, the motion judge stated that he did not credit the defendant’s claim that at the time of the plea, plea counsel advised the defendant that the plea would not affect his immigration status.
… Further, neither the judge’s advisement during the plea colloquy nor the defendant’s written waiver of rights was an adequate substitute for plea counsel’s duty to advise the defendant of the potential dire immigration consequences of his plea.
… Accordingly, plea counsel’s advice regarding the immigration consequences of the defendant’s plea was constitutionally deficient.
His children were all born in the United States, and he discussed the immigration consequences of his plea in order to avoid separation from his wife and children.
text:
Where a defendant’s motion for a new trial was denied, that decision must be reversed because the advice the defendant received regarding the immigration consequences of his guilty plea was constitutionally deficient.

“The defendant … appeals from a Superior Court judge’s order denying his motion for a new trial, claiming that the judge, who was not the plea judge, erred in finding (1) that the defendant did not receive constitutionally deficient advice regarding the immigration consequences of his November 6, 2007 guilty plea, and (2) the defendant was not prejudiced by plea counsel’s advice. We agree and reverse. …

“The defendant argues that the advice he received regarding the immigration consequences of his plea was constitutionally deficient. We agree.

“To be sure, the motion judge stated that he did not credit the defendant’s claim that at the time of the plea, plea counsel advised the defendant that the plea would not affect his immigration status. … Here however, the motion judge did not hear testimony from the parties and supported his credibility determination based on the facts that the plea judge had advised the defendant that his plea ‘may very well have the consequence of your being deported’ and that the defendant signed a waiver of rights acknowledging that his plea ‘could result in my deportation or exclusion from admission to the United States under federal immigration law and that I may be rejected as an applicant for citizenship in the United States.’ The Supreme Judicial Court has recognized that such a colloquy and waiver are ‘not an adequate substitute for defense counsel’s professional obligation to advise [his] client of the likelihood of specific and dire immigration consequences that might result from such a plea.’ …

“While defense counsel may or may not have advised the defendant as to the immigration consequences of his plea, there is nothing to suggest that plea counsel accurately advised the defendant that pleading guilty to a controlled substance offense would subject him to mandatory deportation if apprehended by Federal authorities. … Indeed, the defendant seemingly acted consistently with what he claimed was defense counsel’s advice by traveling to the Dominican Republic. The defendant arguably would not have done so if properly advised of the clear immigration consequences of his conviction, which made him ineligible for readmission to the United States and subject to deportation. …

“In sum, the defendant’s conviction falls squarely within the same statutory provision that the United States Supreme Court held was ‘succinct, clear, and explicit’ regarding its immigration consequences. … Further, neither the judge’s advisement during the plea colloquy nor the defendant’s written waiver of rights was an adequate substitute for plea counsel’s duty to advise the defendant of the potential dire immigration consequences of his plea. … Accordingly, plea counsel’s advice regarding the immigration consequences of the defendant’s plea was constitutionally deficient. …

“The defendant argues that the motion judge erred in finding that plea counsel’s advice did not prejudice the defendant. The defendant emphasizes that the special circumstances indicate that he would have placed particular emphasis on the immigration consequences of his plea to support the conclusion that he was prejudiced. We agree. Although ‘existence of special circumstances does not automatically result in prejudice,’ … a defendant who would have placed particular emphasis on the immigration consequences in deciding whether to plead guilty likewise need not present a viable defense that he would have pursued at trial. …

“Although, as the motion judge noted, ‘the defendant has offered no circumstances where he would not be convicted of a felony’ if the defendant had chosen to go forward to trial, that is not necessarily determinative. …

“While the judge did acknowledge that the special circumstances that the defendant would have placed particular emphasis on the immigration consequences of his plea was a factor in determining whether plea counsel’s performance prejudiced the defendant, his analysis was limited to acknowledging the fact that the defendant is a lawful permanent resident of the United States and noting that lawful permanent resident status does ‘does not necessarily establish’ special circumstances. The judge did not discuss the defendant’s family and life in the United States while considering the defendant’s special circumstances. Thus, we cannot say that the judge gave, as he must, ‘substantial weight’ to the defendant’s special circumstances indicating that he would have prioritized the immigration consequences of his plea. …

“Indeed, the defendant has shown special circumstances that he placed particular emphasis on immigration consequences in deciding whether to plead guilty. … The defendant had been a lawful permanent resident of the United States for almost twenty years at the time of his guilty plea and had been married to a United States citizen for even longer. His children were all born in the United States, and he discussed the immigration consequences of his plea in order to avoid separation from his wife and children. He also had a business and intended to apply for citizenship at the time of his plea (and later did so). …

“Accordingly, the defendant has shown that plea counsel’s advice prejudiced him regarding his decision whether or not to go to trial or to change his plea. …

“The order denying the defendant’s motion to vacate his conviction and for a new trial is reversed. The defendant’s conviction is vacated, and the defendant is to be permitted to withdraw his guilty plea. The case is remanded to the Superior Court for further proceedings if the Commonwealth wishes to seek a new trial.”

Commonwealth v. Pena (Lawyers Weekly No. 81-075-26) (14 pages) (Docket No. 25-P-620) (July 22, 2026).

text:
Harrisburg, PA – Today, Governor Josh Shapiro sued the Trump Administration over its illegal effort to hold millions of critical homeland security dollars hostage in another attempt to control Pennsylvania’s elections.

The lawsuit seeks to stop the unlawful imposition of conditions that require states to change the way they administer elections in order to receive funds awarded through the 2026 Homeland Security Grant Program (HSGP).

The Trump Administration is attempting to restrict 20 percent of states’ total funding to prepare for, protect against, respond to, and recover from catastrophic disasters. As a result, Pennsylvania would lose nearly $6 million in funding to support state, county, and local governments unless it adopted the Trump Administration’s election policy preferences.

This is not the first time that the Trump Administration has tried to withhold homeland security funding from Pennsylvania. Governor Shapiro prevailed in a previous lawsuit after the Trump Administration withheld millions from Pennsylvania’s 2025 HSGP grant.

“The Trump Administration is holding critical funding for homeland security and disaster response hostage in their latest attempt to take over our elections and perpetuate baseless conspiracy theories,” said Governor Shapiro. “Withholding this funding will make our communities less safe and would be dangerous under any circumstance, but doing this in an attempt to undermine states’ authority over elections is reckless and unconstitutional. I’m going to court to protect the people of Pennsylvania from this brazen attempt to withhold vital resources from our law enforcement officers and first responders.”

Among the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)’s new conditions to receive this critical funding are requirements to submit Pennsylvania’s voter registration list and the name of all poll workers to a faulty federal system that has been shown to be unreliable and outdated, transition their voting systems from reliable and proven voting systems to unproven technology shown to result in errors, and to change the Commonwealth’s existing post-election audits to a process that follows nonexistent guidelines set by the Secretary of Homeland Security.

In addition to these unlawful conditions, the lawsuit challenges the Administration’s attempt to reinstate immigration-based conditions for DHS and FEMA funding — nearly identical to those previously struck down. If allowed to continue, states would be forced to devote scarce resources to do the work of the federal government on civil immigration enforcement, beyond what state laws allow or require, in order to receive funding through HSGP and other vital grant emergency management programs.

The lawsuit also challenges the Trump Administration’s decision to condition all 2026 FEMA funding based on the agency’s own assessment of a state’s ability to align with the Administration’s priorities, potentially politicizing emergency responses.

Impact on Local Preparedness

The Homeland Security Grant Program provides essential resources for state and local agencies to:

Train public safety personnel in incident management, threat detection, and emergency response procedures;

Purchase equipment such as chemical and biological detection devices, robotics, drones, and protective gear; and

Maintain communication systems and public messaging infrastructure for coordinated disaster response.

Without this funding, counties and municipalities face significant gaps in their ability to prepare for and respond to emergencies. The loss would:

Limit training and continuing education for emergency managers;

Reduce the number of qualified personnel at state and county levels; and

Undermine communications networks and mutual aid agreements essential to disaster response and recovery.

All 67 counties across Pennsylvania rely on federal HSGP funding to support local emergency management. Established in 2003, the program helps fund critical preparedness and response efforts statewide.

Pennsylvania’s Elections Remain Safe, Secure, Free, and Fair

Since taking office, the Shapiro Administration has promoted the security of the Commonwealth's elections through initiatives like the Administration’s Ready to Vote Toolkit and taken action to defend every Pennsylvanian’s right to vote.

In January 2023, Governor Shapiro appointed Al Schmidt, a Republican, to serve as Secretary of the Commonwealth and oversee Pennsylvania’s elections, promoting the bipartisan administration of elections.

In September 2023, the Governor implemented automatic voter registration (AVR) for eligible Commonwealth residents obtaining driver licenses and ID cards at Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) driver and photo license centers. By taking this step, Pennsylvania joined more than 20 states to promote election security, save taxpayer dollars, and streamline the voter registration process. In April, Republican Auditor General Timothy DeFoor released a report showing the Commonwealth’s AVR system is safe and effective.

In July 2025, Secretary Schmidt announced the Department of State (DOS) had redesigned provisional ballot envelopes for the 2025 general election, leading to an 11.3 percent decrease in the number of ballot rejections due to envelope errors compared to the 2024 cycle.

In April 2026, Governor Shapiro filed a lawsuit challenging President Donald Trump’s signing of Executive Order 14399, which seeks to establish a list of eligible voters through DHS and limit how elections may be conducted by using the United States Post Service (USPS) to illegally and significantly restrict mail-in voting.

Despite the Trump Administration’s now repeated attempts to condition Pennsylvania’s ability to respond to emergencies — and strip state powers to administer elections — the Governor will continue standing up against the overreach of the federal government, protecting Pennsylvanians’ right to vote and ensuring the Commonwealth remains ready to respond to emergencies.

text:
Plainclothes federal officers violently arrested a Ukrainian woman at San Francisco International Airport on Wednesday, according to a video that has gone viral on social media.

Footage of the incident posted on social media shows a woman on the ground actively being detained by several men. The woman can be heard yelling in distress that they are choking her and that they are ICE officers seeking to deport her.

“Stop, stop!” She can be heard yelling on the video. “Let me go. Please help me. Leave me alone!”

The detention happened near what appear to be restaurants and shops inside the passenger terminal at SFO, and several witnesses can be heard pleading with police to stop. One person could be heard asking, “What are you arresting her for?”

The video was posted by Richmond City Council Member Doria Robinson, who told the Chronicle she was first alerted to the arrest by the woman’s screams for help as she waited to board a flight to Seattle. She called what unfolded “unreal.”

The men were not in uniform, Robinson said, and did not identify themselves. At first, she said she wondered if it was domestic violence. Then, as hordes of people gathered to watch — some recording and trying to get the woman’s name and a contact number — it became clear what was happening, the council member said.

A spokesperson for SFO said the airport was not involved in federal law enforcement operations, “nor are we notified when they occur.”

State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, condemned the arrest in a statement, saying ICE was deporting a woman home back to “the front line of a war zone” in Ukraine.

“ICE’s terror campaign against our communities must end. Iryna Gorb made a home in San Francisco and is one of many people who help make San Francisco run,” said Wiener, who is running for a Congressional seat. “Trump’s terror machine has no place in California and neither does ICE.”

text:
Each day, dozens of immigrants from across the Southwest are required to travel to El Paso for their check-ins at the Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Service Processing Center.

They are driving in from hundreds of miles away — as far as Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Odessa and Midland — often with only a day's notice.

The immigrants disappear inside the secured federal complex at the corner of Montano Avenue and Mattox Street in East-Central El Paso. Their loved ones anxiously wait outside of the main security gate, worried about whether the immigrant is going to be released.

"When people are told that they're going to have to go to down to El Paso for a check-in, not only is it extremely difficult that you'll have to take a day or two off work or have to pay for travel and a hotel, but it's also just terrifying for people," Zoe Bowman, a lawyer with the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center, said.

"There is a risk of people being detained at their ICE check-ins and we can never advise a client that they definitely will or definitely won't. But there is a certain risk."

Immigrants have been required to travel to El Paso from across West Texas and New Mexico for their check-ins since February 2026, Leticia Zamarripa, ICE's El Paso sector spokeswoman, said. The ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Field Office in El Paso took over case management of non-detained immigration cases for the entire area of responsibility, she explained.

"Like almost all law enforcement agencies, operational changes sometimes occur to efficiently fulfill our mission of arresting and removing illegal and subject to removal aliens from American communities," Zamarripa said. "ICE has arrested aliens who are amenable for detention or have violated or absconded from their Alternative to Detention appointments. Others have been released on ATD after review on a case-by-case basis."

The El Paso Times has spoken with dozens of immigrants and their family members from across the Southwest who have expressed frustration with the short notice of the location change and that they are not permitted to accompany their loved ones inside.

Many of the immigrants traveling to El Paso are from Cuba, Venezuela, Mexico, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Cameroon who are seeking their green cards because their loved one is a legal U.S. resident or a citizen and for those with a pending asylum or refugee case.

'I was so scared'

Traveling to El Paso is unnerving for many immigrants who have had to make the trek for their required check-in.

One immigrant, who requested anonymity out of fear of reprisals by ICE, was filled with fear when she arrived in El Paso earlier this month.

"I was so scared," the 30-year-old Cuban said. "I didn't know where the address was, so I looked it up and I saw it was a detention center. It was even worse. Horrible things came to mind."

She lives just outside Midland, Texas, where she previously made her scheduled check-ins with ICE. But two weeks ago, she was informed that the Midland field office was closing and that she would need to travel nearly five hours to El Paso for her check-in.

She entered the United States through the Biden administration's parole program for Cubans four years ago, married her husband and filed an I-130 immigration application for family unification in early 2025.

The I-130 process is the first step immigrants take to obtain a family-based U.S. green card. A lawful citizen or a permanent resident files a petition to have a family member join them in the United States.

In some cases, immigrants who have been in the U.S. with their family members have arrived for these types of immigration check-ins only to be greeted by ICE agents who notify them they must return to their home countries while awaiting the I-130 approval process, which used to take 12 to 14 months.

Currently, the U.S. Citizens and Immigrations Services estimates that the process is taking long, up 11 to 12 years for a U.S. resident to bring their a family member1-130 relief. The Trump administration has paused issuing visas for 74 countries including on immigrants from Cuba, Venezuela and Guatemala.

She traveled with her husband, who also is Cuban, and their U.S. baby girl to El Paso.

When she arrived, she joined over a dozen other immigrants at 8 a.m. waiting at the main gate for their appointments. Her husband waited across the street, where he stood the entire time she was inside.

She was inside for nearly five hours and was given another appointment by the agent who attended to her case. She wasn't detained, but being taken into custody during a check-in is always a threat.

Most immigrants are sent to ICE's Intensive Supervision Appearance Program — private contractors run the program and it is an alternative to being detained — on Boeing Avenue to be fitted with an ankle monitor.

There are 1,326 in the ATD program in El Paso as of July 11, according to ICE's data.

Increasing ICE enforcement operations in Texas

There has been a sharp increase in immigration enforcement operations across the United States. Recent ICE data suggests that they have been detaining around 1,500 immigrants per day.

Texas is at the center of new immigration enforcement operations. Cities such as Dallas, Houston, San Antonio and Harlingen are seeing an acceleration in immigration enforcement operations, Jessica Cisneros of the Texas Immigration Law Council said.

"Texas really is dominating the national picture," Cisneros said.

El Paso saw an increase in immigration enforcement operations, according to an analysis of ICE's data by Austin Kocher, an immigration researcher and professor at Syracuse University. There were around 2,500 ICE arrests made in El Paso alone between Jan. 1 and March 9, according to the data.

Monitored around the clock

The young mother left her check-in and was reunited with her husband in an emotional release of anxiety. But she wasn't able to return home just yet.

She was sent to the ISAP and left with a new ankle monitor. The family departed El Paso in the afternoon and finally made it home late at night, she said.

The ankle monitor allows immigration agents to track immigrants' locations and movement history via Global Positioning Systems. It is one of three options ICE is using to keep tabs on immigrants who are not detained, though it does not always guarantee they will not be detained in the future.

The whole process has been draining for her and her family, especially as she had to pass through an immigration checkpoint leaving for Midland. But she still fears leaving her house to go to the market.

"It has been a nightmare," she said. "You have to have a strong mind to survive this whole process."

text:
SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- A Ukrainian woman was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at San Francisco International Airport on Wednesday, according to the Department of Homeland Security and a friend who says she later called him from a detention facility.

Video of the arrest posted on Facebook by Richmond City Councilmember Doria Robinson, shows Iryna Gorb asking for help as agents detain her at the airport.

Andy Eblin, who said he has known Gorb for about 15 years, told ABC7 Eyewitness News he received a call from her Wednesday night.

"I picked it up it was her at the detention facility in Stockton," Eblin said. "She let me know how she was doing was alright and that she was detained at SFO while deboarding a flight from Portland."

Eblin said Gorb has lived in the United States throughout the time he has known her and said that was working to find her- hoping to speak with her again.

MORE: United investigates after agent allegedly threatened to call ICE on passenger at SFO

"It was a brief call- she sounded alright, honestly more in shock than anything else," he said. "She didn't seem like she had full insight into what was going on. She told me that she believes she is going to be transferred to Cal City."

In a statement to ABC7 Eyewitness News, the Department of Homeland Security said:

"On July 22, ICE arrested Iryna Gorb, an illegal alien from Ukraine at the San Francisco International Airport. When officers approached Gorb, she attempted to flee and resisted arrest.... Gorb overstayed her visa and remained in the United States illegally for 15 years in violation of our nation's laws. She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings."

ABC7 Eyewitness News also asked DHS about what appeared to be agents wearing plain clothes in the video.

The inquiry follows scrutiny over ICE agent identification stemming from recent incidents, including fatal shootings and a botched plainclothes arrest in Las Vegas. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously reported that current requirements call for agents to wear identifiable field attire, including clearly visible badges.

DHS did not provide an explanation regarding the attire of the agents shown in the video.

text:
A Los Angeles family’s pursuit of criminal charges for an off-duty ICE agent who fatally shot their loved one on New Years Eve highlights a question communities face amid the recent spate of killings of civilians by federal agents: Will LA’s elected prosecutors criminally charge federal immigration agents if they unlawfully kill someone?

After more than 17,860 arrests of immigrants in the LA County region over the last year, and at least four shootings in LA by Department of Homeland Security agents, residents want immigration agents held accountable when they act violently or unlawfully.

The family of Keith Porter Jr. is demanding that LA County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman press criminal charges against ICE agent Brian Palacios.

Palacios shot Porter, a father of two daughters, at an apartment complex in Northridge after the 43-year-old fired a gun into the air the night of Dec. 31 to celebrate the new year.

Immigrant defense groups and the families of other people killed or harmed by DHS agents across the U.S. are calling for DHS agents to be criminally charged, removed from public life, and stripped of federal funding.

After DHS agents killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop in Houston on July 7, the region’s prosecutor said he’d criminally charge ICE agents if he found criminal wrongdoing.

Salgado Araujo and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, an immigrant who was also fatally shot in a traffic stop this month by federal immigration agents in Maine, were the 29th and 30th people shot by immigration agents since President Donald Trump took office last year.

“We’re dealing with an administration that is not giving up in its terror campaign against our immigrant and refugee communities,” said Sergio Perez, a former U.S. Justice Department civil rights trial attorney who recently served as the executive director of the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law. “We’ve seen, following ICE or DHS related shootings, an effort to seek out accountability and that families and individuals get justice. I would hope that weighs heavily on the [LA] district attorney’s office.”

Will the LA district attorney prosecute ICE agents who break the law?

It remains unclear whether Hochman, a former Republican who chided progressive criminal justice reforms when he was elected in 2024, will criminally charge Palacios, or any other federal agents who may’ve committed crimes.

During the surge in immigration operations in LA County last June, Hochman released a statement acknowledging the “fear” ICE raids cause and promising to tackle crimes that “affect public safety—regardless of a person’s background.”

On Tuesday, LA County DA spokesperson Greg Risling said in an email to LA Public Press that public prosecutors are still reviewing the case.

“Our experienced prosecutors will conduct a thorough analysis of all the facts and evidence to determine whether criminal charges can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” the email said. “Given the complexity of that process, it is difficult to predict a timeline for completion, and cases like this can take several months or more to resolve.”

Risling didn’t answer a question asking if federal agencies have cooperated with the DA during the investigation.

Jsané Tyler, Porter’s cousin, said at a July 15 press conference hosted by Black Lives Matter-LA (BLM-LA) that Porter’s family and their allies will continue to press Hochman to promptly prosecute the case.

“He was murdered on New Year’s Eve, and here we are in July, finally with the case moving to the DA’s Office,” Tyler said. “Make no mistake, we’re going to continue to come out here and take action until our family can rest.”

In February, Tyler and BLM-LA delivered a petition with more than 18,600 signatures to the LA Board of Police Commissioners demanding the LA Police Department and Hochman investigate Palacios.

The LAPD said in an email Tuesday to LA Public Press that the agency completed its investigation of the Porter shooting and submitted its findings to Hochman on June 29.

“[The DA] will review the case and determine if criminal charges are warranted,” the email said. The agency didn’t provide a name for a spokesperson and didn’t answer whether federal law enforcement agencies were compliant during the investigation.

DHS didn’t respond to an LA Public Press email Tuesday asking whether Palacios is still employed by ICE, whether he’s been assigned to a different region, and whether DHS is working with local law enforcement to investigate the shooting.

Will the CA attorney general prosecute ICE agents if the LA district attorney refuses to do so?

Perez, the civil rights attorney, told LA Public Press that if Hochman declines to criminally charge Palacios, Porter’s family and BLM-LA activists could ask California Attorney General Rob Bonta to review the case.

After federal agencies refused to cooperate with Minnesota prosecutors on investigations into the ICE killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, Bonta issued a guidance saying local law enforcement agencies like the LAPD and LA County DA have the authority to investigate and prosecute federal agents who have violated state law.

“California stands ready to take all necessary steps to investigate potentially unlawful conduct by federal agents that occurs on our soil, and where the facts warrant, file charges for violations of [state law],” Bonta said in a Jan. 27 press release announcing the guidance.

But Perez, formerly the head of oversight for Orange County’s law enforcement, said he isn’t confident Bonta would charge Palacios or any other federal agents who break the law.

“That is not a very likely thing to happen,” said Perez. “History in this county and in our state speaks to a general aversion to hold law enforcement accountable, whether they were acting on duty or off duty.”

If Hochman doesn’t move forward with a criminal case against Palacios, Perez said that would make it easier for Bonta to do the same.

“If you have the district attorney’s office look at a tragedy and say, ‘We’re not going to do anything about it,’ that makes it much easier for the state attorney general’s office to also sadly wash their hands of any responsibility here,” Perez said.

Asked Tuesday whether Bonta would prosecute the Porter case if Hochman declines to bring criminal charges forward, AG spokesperson Alexandra Duquet said in an email that the agency declined to comment.

“To protect their integrity, we can’t comment on, even to confirm or deny, potential or ongoing investigations,” Duquet said.

Melina Abdullah, an activist with BLM-LA, said in a text message Wednesday to LA Public Press the grassroots organization is focused on pressing Hochman to charge Palacios but remains open to other remedies.

“We are focusing our current efforts on pushing the district attorney to do his job and prosecute,” Abdullah said. “We also remain open to all avenues that can bring justice in Keith Porter’s name.”

Perez said the decision before Hochman, and Bonta, presents an opportunity for prosecutors to signal what lengths they’ll go to protect people from federal agents who unlawfully kill or harm the public.

“Press releases and interview comments are one thing, but where it really matters is seeing a commitment of [DA Hochman and AG Bonta] to keep Californians safe,” Perez said. “California has been in the crosshairs of the Trump administration’s massive and violent immigration [enforcement] and deportation machine, and it would be really telling to see [Bonta and Hochman] step up and match action to rhetoric.”

text:
Nearly a year after the Trump administration launched Operation Midway Blitz, a new national report alleges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection agents committed widespread civil rights violations last year.

The ACLU research report, titled Agents of Chaos and Cruelty, examined immigration enforcement in 2025 across eight states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Louisiana, Maryland and New Mexico.

The authors examined more than 1,200 incidents and found more than 400 involving activity they consider misconduct, such as use of force, intimidation or retaliation. Almost half of the incidents involving misconduct were in Illinois. The ACLU compiled the information using a variety of sources, including news coverage, court filings and public statements from federal agencies.

"We saw some of the harshest use of those kind of militaristic tactics here as opposed to elsewhere," said Ed Yohnka, director of communications and public policy for the ACLU of Illinois.

The Mexican government announced this month it would take legal action over 17 Mexican citizens who they say died as a result of ICE enforcement, including 14 in detention centers and three during ICE operations.

The Illinois incidents cited by the ACLU happened most often outside of homes and in neighborhoods, during traffic stops, during street stops and at big box hardware stores. Of those detained or targeted, 77 were adult U.S. citizens.

NBC 5 Investigates reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, ICE and Border Patrol to ask about the report but did not hear back.

The Trump administration rolled back the Biden-era policy that prevented ICE and Border Patrol from operating at sensitive locations, like schools, hospitals and shelters. The report shows in Illinois, there were 37 incidents at sensitive locations.

"The cruelty that was put in place here by saying there is nowhere that's safe -- not a school, not a hospital, nowhere that's safe -- is that it it constricted the way in which people live their lives," Yohnka said.

Yohnka was also troubled by how Illinois young adults were affected by immigration agents. More than 50 people who were detained or targeted were under the age of 21.

"We don't know what the harm, the psychological harm, is for those children and those families, and we're not going to know for a number of years," Yohnka said.

Ultimately, he believes it's important to document this history and think about what enforcement might look like in the future.

"We need to turn away from ICE as it has been structured under the Department of Homeland Security," Yohnka said.
